item.title: NFL Panic Meter: History isn't on side of 0-2 Colts and Shane Steichen. Playing it safe in OT vs. Patrick Mahomes could cost him
item.description: Steichen might have the hottest seat among all NFL head coaches, unless it belongs to Todd Bowles.
item.content:encoded:
Shane Steichen failed to make the playoffs in each of his first three seasons coaching the Indianapolis Colts, and many teams wouldn't be patient enough to give him a fourth shot at it.

The Colts brought back Steichen and general manager Chris Ballard, but Colts CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon made it very clear that time was running out. During her postseason media conference she said: "I'm pissed. We're all pissed."

"We have been very clear with Chris and Shane that giving them another opportunity means that the sense of urgency for them to deliver and perform has never been higher," Irsay-Gordon said.

While all teams who start 0-2 should be worried, it seems especially ominous for Steichen.

The Colts fought hard in Sunday night's game at Kansas City, but that wasn't the focus after the Chiefs won in overtime. It was Steichen's decision to kick a field goal and tie the game in overtime, giving Patrick Mahomes more than enough time to drive downfield and win it. He did, and the Colts lost 33-30. It was the ninth straight loss for the Colts. The hot start of last season is long forgotten.

The issues in overtime started with two straight runs to Jonathan Taylor that lost 3 yards just as the Colts had driven deep into Chiefs' territory. It's reasonable considering Taylor is Indianapolis' best player, but it looked bad when the Colts suddenly faced a third-and-13.

"I was trying to finish the game with JT, put the ball in his hands," Steichen said, via the team's site.

When Indianapolis faced a fourth-and-8, there was a decision to be made. A field goal would likely result in a tie at best considering there was a little more than three minutes remaining. And the Colts, with a defense that has given up a league-worst 1,029 yards this season, gave Mahomes a chance to win with a field goal. It's not completely unreasonable to kick the field goal in that spot, but it looks bad if it doesn't work.

Steichen said the Colts were going to run a fourth-down play but only if the Chiefs lined up with a defensive look they were hoping for. When the Colts didn't like the defensive look they got, Steichen called a timeout and took the field goal.

Like the rest of Steichen's Colts tenure, it was close to being good, and that's not going to cut it. Steichen went 9-8 his first season and 8-9 in each of the two seasons after that. Last season was cruel with a 7-1 start that fell apart, especially after Daniel Jones tore his Achilles. It's clear Jones is still working back from that injury and not at his best yet, which makes it tough on the Colts and Steichen. But the NFL doesn't care much about excuses, and Steichen already got one pass for Jones' injury last season. Only 24 of 200 (12%) of teams that started the season 0-2 made the playoffs from 2002-25, according to USA Today. If the Colts don't make the playoffs for the fourth time in Steichen's four seasons, there's a good chance Irsay-Gordon will feel compelled to make a change. The odds are against him, like they were when he gave Mahomes a chance to win Sunday night.

Panic meter: Steichen might have the hottest seat among all NFL head coaches, unless it belongs to Todd Bowles.

How much trouble is Todd Bowles in?

The Buccaneers losing to the Browns on Sunday was miserable. It wouldn't have been good regardless of what came before it, but the loss being a continuation of all the Buccaneers' issues since the middle of last season is a really bad look for Bowles.

Bowles is 35-35 as Buccaneers head coach. While that's not terrible, he's trending in the wrong direction. Last season, the Buccaneers went from 6-2 to blowing the NFC South, which was one of the worst divisions in NFL history. They finished 8-9. This season they're off to an 0-2 start. Tampa Bay lost the opener at Cincinnati, and it was a winnable game if the Bucs didn't have four turnovers. They were sloppy again on Sunday against a Browns team that was blown out in Week 1, and have been sloppy in most games since that 6-2 start in 2025.

What stands out is Tampa Bay's defense let Deshaun Watson beat it. Watson had his best game, in terms of EPA per play, of his Browns career. Bowles is a defensive coach and he hasn't had a defense rank in the top half of the league in yards and points allowed since 2022.

Bowles probably was close to being fired after last season's collapse. But Tampa Bay brought him back, and the early season results are poor. Losing to the Browns has to be unacceptable. It's early in the season, but not too early to have a close eye on Bowles' job security if Tampa Bay doesn't turn things around fast.

Panic meter: The Buccaneers' next three opponents are the Vikings, Packers and Cowboys and it might be bad for Bowles to lose all three. Or maybe even two.

Maybe we should consider Dan Quinn, too

When a head coach fires both coordinators, there's only one more move to make if things don't turn around.

Quinn parted ways with his offensive and defensive coordinators after going 5-12 last season. The Commanders had a tough early-season schedule, starting with divisional road games against the Eagles and Cowboys. Washington went 0-2, and had a competitive loss at Philadelphia, but it's impossible to feel positive after Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow again.

Daniels injured the elbow on the final play of the first half, and he's seeing specialists before the Commanders announce a timetable for his return. If Daniels misses a month or more, what will the Commanders' record look like when he's back? And will he have a different head coach if it gets really bad?

Panic meter: Quinn might not be in immediate danger, but the seat could get hotter if Daniels misses time and the losses pile up.

How bad will this get for Chargers?

Being 0-2 is bad. Being 0-2, with losses to the Cardinals and Raiders, when your next seven opponents are the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos, Chiefs, Rams, Texans and Ravens? That could be a death sentence for the Chargers' season.

The Chargers are off to a miserable start. Everything has been bad to open the season. They've lost as a big favorite twice at home and there are no positives on either side of the ball. This is really bad. It might be impossible to turn this around before it's too late.

Panic meter: An0-9 start isn't likely, but it's not impossible either.

Is the Packers' offense going to be OK?

In the first 90 seconds of Sunday's game, receiver Jayden Reed was carted off with a back injury and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele left on the cart with a knee injury. Reed should miss time and Bako-Bewele might miss the rest of the season. It's not like the Packers' offense was in good shape before that.

The offensive line is as shaky as any in the NFL at this point. It was so thin Sunday the Packers almost had to use tight end Tucker Kraft at tackle. The line can't protect Jordan Love, who had just 145 yards passing vs. the Jets.

The running game is a mess without Josh Jacobs. MarShawn Lloyd has seemingly botched his opportunity; he was essentially benched after six carries and a fumble on Sunday. Kaleb Johnson got some extra carries, but he's far from a sure thing after the Steelers gave up on him just one year after making him a third-round draft pick.

The Packers rallied to avoid an 0-2 start. And a Thursday night game against the Falcons could be a get-right spot. But it's worrisome in Green Bay right now.

Panic meter: Getting higher and will be a five-alarm fire if they lose to the Falcons.

Drake Maye's slump continues

Mike Vrabel was just annoyed at a question after a win, but his answer to a postgame question about Maye's lackluster performance on Sunday was fairly telling.

"You're not going to ruin my Sunday, but I'll come back to you tomorrow," Vrabel said. "Thanks, bud."

Imagine Vrabel saying last season that his Sunday would have been ruined by having to talk about Maye.

Maye's slump that goes back to last postseason has been an ongoing topic, and it didn't get cured against the Steelers. Maye had 208 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. The Patriots scored just one offensive touchdown in a 20-3 win.

Maye is off to a slow start this season, as is New England's offense. It won't be easy to break out with A.J. Brown out for a while either. But it's also not like Maye's near-MVP season didn't happen. He's a good quarterback, albeit an inexperienced one that is having to make some adjustments.

Panic meter: No reason to give up on Maye yet, but it would be nice to see a big game soon.

item.title: Lukas Van Ness has arrived
item.description: Van Ness is paying off the Packers’ patience.
item.content:encoded:
Lukas Van Ness had an inauspicious start to his NFL career. Through two seasons, he’d produced just seven sacks and 16 quarterback hits. He was solid against the run, but you don’t pick an edge rusher 13th overall because he’s stout in the ground game.

Year three was promising, but then the injuries came. Nagging issues limited Van Ness to just nine games in 2025, and for more than a few of those nine, he clearly wasn’t quite himself. 

And then the Packers picked up his fifth-year option this past offseason. I was a fan of the move, but I can understand anybody who was skeptical. Injuries and a lack of production are a recipe for some negativity, and Van Ness had plenty of both of those things.

But through two weeks, Van Ness has paid off every bit of faith the Packers have had in him. Two weeks does not a season make (and the Packers are thanking the ghost of Lombardi for that), but the start for Van Ness is about as promising as things could be. Hopefully this turns into a season-long trend. The Van Ness ascension may just have begun.

item.title: Nick Sirianni thinks the Eagles’ run game is close
item.description: The Eagles head coach lauds Cam Jurgens sacrifice to change positions, and talks about the run game struggles.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles run game has struggled through two games to open the 2026 season, and that was the main focus when head coach Nick Sirianni spoke to reporters on Monday, following the team’s win in Tennessee.

Sirianni highlighted the sacrifice that Cam Jurgens made by being willing to move over to left guard, acknowledging that the majority of his time this offseason and through training camp was at the center position. He noted that there are opportunities for some cross training within walkthroughs, and Jurgens did play right guard in the past.

“But, [Cam Jurgens] sure got a lot of reps this week at [left guard] and thought he came out against a really good defensive front and played a solid game.”

As for the slow start for the Eagles run game, Sirianni said that it’s a collaborative effort, from coaches to players, so it’s not just on the running backs or offensive linemen. He explained that it takes every player on the field to be successful in the run game, and it’s a full team effort to be better – which he knows they are capable of doing. 

“And we’re close. We are close. But it goes back to when you’re close, it’s never just one thing. It’s the entire group working as a whole. We have to be committed to it still and keep grinding away at it, but we know we have room to improve there in our run game.”

The head coach also talked about the number of negative plays through two games, to which he pointed mostly to the run game, but also blamed penalties and sacks. 

“Negative plays, you always want to stay on track. It’s hard to move the ball forward. Let’s say you get a kickoff at the 30-yard line, and you’ve got to go 70 yards. Well, it’s hard to go those 70 yards if you’re moving backwards. Regardless of if it’s a sack, a negative run, a penalty, even a drop pass that doesn’t move it forward at all, a missed throw, whatever it may be; It’s hard to go the length of the field when you’re moving backwards. That’s always going to be a point of emphasis of what we need to do.”

Sirianni took an opportunity to applaud Tank Bigsby for always playing extremely hard and having some dirty runs. 

“I think about that one that’s down near the goal line where he keeps his feet driving and gets us all the way down to the three and then caps it off [with] the touchdown. Obviously, a great sequence there for Tank. Tank made a tackle on special teams yesterday on punt that was pretty awesome to see. Tank’s a guy that constantly — he’s such a good teammate and he’s constantly doing the little things he needs to do to help the team win. It’s great to see him be rewarded with a touchdown yesterday and a couple nice runs. You knew he would be ready to go. I thought he played solidly.”

item.title: Pattern Degradations and Bad Dresses; Miami Dolphins stumble against 49ers
item.description: Dolphins continue slow start in week two.
item.content:encoded:
Wow! I wrote about pattern recognition last week and boy did I see some patterns. Bad ones. My grandmother was a seamstress by trade and watching her work when I was boy was very educational. She said “Paul, cut out this pattern section for a dress or blouse and then I will sew them together and measure for the final fitting. Measure twice. Cut once.” Basic stuff. That was the first time I ever heard the word “pattern.” I did my best but, my grandmother always said you can undercut the pattern but never overcut the pattern because I can’t add the small sections back and the blouse will look silly.

This Miami Dolphins team is a bad pattern that is overcut, undercut and not measured properly. Yes, we have terrible scissors, materials and needles. IMHO, this situation is worse than Flores’ first season. Why yes, the situation is different. But I don’t see much to build upon. We should be able to see one small but strong piece. Maybe I just don’t see it. But like back then under Flores, this is a “start from the foundation process” but I feel more scared. The question is why. Darryl Johnston made great points about the “process.” and we have to be okay with suffering under the process. And I get it but I don’t get mistakes from nearly every single position group.  

Sunday, against the 49ers, it is very hard to tell if it is the talent (or lack thereof) or the schemes/coaching. There were so many bad mistakes that I am not sure where to start to fix. There were simply numerous blown assignments, numerous lack of playmakings and numerous “out-classings.” Example, Michael Taafe tried to go high on Deebo Samuel or George Kittle (can’t remember) and fell off like a baby stroller trying to tackle a freight train. Welcome to the NFL, rookie! Before going any further on the defense, I will give a 15% curve upgrade score to the entire secondary because the pass rush is completely non-existent. We have zero pass-rush talent even when Chop is in there. The last two QBs have not had to worry about getting hit and the WRs know they can run all of their “ingenious routes” according to Darryl Johnston. This is simply ludicrous because ANY offensive system will work, when there is no pressure on the QB or on the RBs. Darryl Johnston probably knows this but has to build up Brock Purdy and Kyle Shanahan to prop up the NFL lore of how great the players are. Brock Purdy isn’t one-tenth the QB that Dan Marino was. He can run, yes, but his throws are all perimeter precision throws backed by a superior rushing attack. I really do like Brock Purdy but the Wing-T or Run-n-Shoot would have worked perfectly well again this defense. How do we fix the defense? What if we had very good players at every position? Could this coaching staff coach them up? You can’t blame every single defensive SNAFU on the players, many yes but not all of them. What new breakdowns will we see next week against Mahomes? Rest assured, we will see Mr. Kenneth Walker ad infinitum.

My last column mentioned how special teams should be the easiest thing to fix. Boy was I wrong!!!!! This punter can’t even hold on to a ball to punt it. How does this happen? Lack of concentration, I think. Yes, I still believe they are using the “K” balls which were originally supposed to come out of the box and handed to the kicker right before it was kicked. I think the NFL has eased up on that (please correct me) so the ball is slickish( I just coined that word ). Last week we couldn’t stop the long returns; for now that seems to be fixed. For now. I should wager which special teams mistake(s) will we make next week. Why in the name of Garo Yepremian has one of our kicker/punter been needed to make a tackle the first two weeks? Who is in charge of special teams? This takes me back to the trepidation about coaching. I contend that special teams is one-third of the game. If you come out neutral on special teams, that is good enough for me. At the National Championship at the Rose Bowl, I watched Auburn lose to FSU on two game changing special teams plays: a fake punt AND a kickoff return. Other than that, Auburn was better than FSU but FSU DOMINATED special teams and deserved to beat Auburn. I don’t want that to happen to the Dolphins and I don’t want mediocrity to be accepted on special teams, offense or defense.

item.title: Miami Dolphins Week 2 reactions: Tuesday Miami Thoughts With The Earl
item.description: That was… something.
item.content:encoded:
That was… I mean… well… what can I say about that?  I had zero expectations about a win, but I hoped it would be somewhat competitive.  It was not.  That just plain sucked.  That is all.  Thank you for reading.

Oh, you’re still here?  In that case, I’ll hit on a few things I noticed from a quick watch of the game.  As usge, I will preface by saying the best way to dissect the game if through All-22 film, which I will not get to watch today.

Setting the table

This loss sucked, but let’s look at it with some aqua-colored glasses for a moment.  The 49ers are a Super Bowl contender.  The Dolphins are not.  There was plenty of discussion this week about the total number of Pro Bowls on the San Francisco 49ers roster versus the Miami Dolphins roster.  There was the payroll discrepancy discussion.  The broadcast highlighted how the 49ers were the oldest team in the league facing the youngest team in the league.  The week prior, the 49ers went across the world to face the Los Angeles Super Rams and left with a 27-7 win.  Reigning MVP Matthew Stafford went 15-of-25, 155 yards, no touchdowns, one interception, a passer rating of 61.2, and a QBR of 37.5.  He had current 1st-team All-Pro Puka Nacua and three-time 1st-team All-Pro Davante Adams.  They were limited to 290 yards of offense, 2-9 on 3rd down, and ran 57 total plays.  The Super Rams defense allowed 379 total yards, 27 points, and generated 3 pressures with no sacks despite having the reigning DPOY and single-season sack leader Myles Garrett on their team.  The Super Rams were considered THE top contender for the Super Bowl championship this season, and they were shut down by the 49ers.

Enter the rebuilding Dolphins.  They have a QB with limited NFL snaps, 3 rookie WRs, a ton of rookies on the defensive side of the ball, and are considered THE top contender for the 1st overall draft pick.  Remember back in the day when kids would make those paper shuriken?  The Dolphins brought THAT to a nuclear war.  Calling this an unfair fight is an understatement.  Still, the Dolphins produced 284 yards of offense, were 7-15 on 3rd downs, and Willis had an arguably better stat line than Stafford against this same team in THEIR building.

My point is that fans should not view this through the lens of how far away the Dolphins are from contention.  We know that – and more on that later.  The point is that the 49ers did the same thing to a far superior opponent the week before, and they’ll likely do it to others most weeks.

The offense can move the ball

One of the few positives from this game is that the Dolphins offense showed they can move the ball.  At least in the first half.  The Dolphins controlled the clock and generated 155 of their 284 yards in 3 drives. I don’t think it would have changed the outcome, but how different would it have felt if they could have scored a TD or two on those drives?  Imagine if they entered halftime 17-14, 14-13, or 14-10 instead of 14-6.  I don’t think the defense was stopping the 49ers at all, but let’s say the score after the 49ers’ opening 2nd-half drive is 21-14.  Wouldn’t that change how the offense plays?  Instead of being down 21-6 and having to force things, they could run a more balanced offense and grind down the clock.  Maybe the score still ends up wild, but we would feel a little better knowing they performed well against a top tier opponent.

The non-existent pass rush

The elephant in the stadium for this Dolphins team isn’t the secondary or Malik Willis.  It’s the pass rush that does not exist. Pro Football Focus did not have the advanced stats at the time of writing, but they now show Miami had two QB hits.  That’s it.  Purdy had all day to throw, and it showed.  He had only two incompletions that day.  The San Francisco OL is pretty good, and they limited the LA Super Rams to 3 pressures, so let’s not forget that part.  But the Dolphins did not generate much pass rush against the Raiders last week.  PFF has a preseason ranking of offensive lines, and Miami only plays 1 team listed outside their top 20 – Green Bay at 27th.  They face 8 of the top 11 ranked OLs, including the two games against Buffalo (6th) and New England (11th).  Based on a quick Google search, the lowest number of sacks ever recorded in a season was the 1956 Packers with 9.  In recent history, the 2008 Chiefs only recorded 10 sacks.  The 2026 Dolphins will be flirting with this record.  I can’t see a game soon where the Dolphins have a good opportunity to get a sack.  The Chiefs have a good OL and a QB that can avoid sacks well.  The Vikings also have a good OL.  This secondary needs all the help it can get and without any pressure up front, games are going to look more like this one.

This and that

  • Caleb Douglas was quiet, then got injured.  That’s bad news for a team that has nothing at pass catcher.  Chris Bell is still working his way back, and he should become a bigger factor.  But no one else can get open.  Turns out having adequate offensive skill players IS important.
  • Willie Gay Jr. had too many mistakes in this game, and his playing time should be reduced.  In fairness, I would expect a rookie like Trey Moore to make mistakes.  But WGJ is a veteran and at this point, should be depth and not a starter.
  • Malik Willis is making some inexperienced mistakes that need to be cleaned up.  He ran out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage not once, but twice.  Those should be throwaways.  Those lose yardage and count as sacks on the stat sheet.  The box score says he sacked 4 times, but only 2 of those were actual defenders getting him to the ground.  These moments are coaching moments, and I kinda understand what he may be thinking.  He’s likely thinking “I can make it on the run”, but that window closes quick.  He is also missing some throws he should not miss. But that may be because of…
  • The offensive line sucks again.  Namely, the right tackle position.  Willis and the Dolphins cannot drop back into standard passing situations without getting pressure almost immediately.  Jackson is healthy but has now become a liability.  For what he gives you in the running game, you lose in pass protection.  At some point, the Dolphins really need to consider moving Kadyn Proctor to RT and letting DJ Campbell start at LG.  I know that goes against what they said earlier this offseason, but the status quo isn’t working.  Caedan Wallace may be the next guy up, but he hasn’t shown enough to feel confident he’ll be an upgrade.
  • The Dolphins may be patient with Jackson, but they may also trade him as soon as they feel it’s necessary.  Jackson will not be back in 2027.  The Dolphins recently amended his contract, which makes it easier to trade him this season.  Now, they won’t get much for him.  Maybe a later-round pick swap or perhaps a player-for-player swap.  But in a season where the Dolphins will not be competitive, getting something for a player who will be leaving anyway would be a smart move for the GM to make.

I said what I said

Ok… here is the “more on that later” material.  I could write a couple of articles about the draft, free agency, and stuff like positional value.  I will wait until the appropriate time for that.  But after two weeks, some areas of need for the 2027 offseason are obvious.  The Dolphins will need a new right tackle.  They will need 2 new edge rushers.  There are a few more needs that may become apparent.  That is wide receiver, cornerback, safety, guard, tight end, and sigh… quarterback.

Last week, I mentioned that Hafley could be on the hot seat quickly if the Dolphins go winless.  In a glitch in the matrix, even ct1361 agrees with me. Sorta.  I’m not saying he SHOULD be fired, but that is a problem for another day.  Back during the draft season, I mentioned how a poorly ran draft could be an indicator of how long this rebuild process will go.  I was very much against drafting OL in the 1st round because in general, one individual OL will not have the impact that a skill position player will.  Caleb Douglas, if he continues to be a hit, will impact the win/loss total more than Kadyn Proctor will if he is a hit.  Now, we can argue this until the cows come home and I really don’t want to rehash any of that now – that’s a draft time discussion. 

The part of that discussion I want to focus on is the time frame.  The Dolphins have 2 major issues entering the 2027 offseason, and possibly a 3rd issue.

The first is a principle issue.  The Dolphins and Jon-Eric Sullivan have stated they want to build through the draft.  That’s fine.  But that will take a ton of time.  Most draft classes have one or two hits at best.  The Dolphins had a league high 13 draft picks in 2026.  If half of them hit, that’s essentially a complete class.  That’s wonderful.  But no one bats 1.000 in this area and Sully will have his share of misses.  He does not have 13 draft picks in 2027.  Right now, Miami has 8 picks in 2027, with an extra 5th coming from Pittsburgh. Those will not be enough to put Miami into immediate contention. 

In addition to Sully wanting to build through the draft, he also says he wants to use free agency in a very directed manner.  He’s not going to spend willy-nilly.  During the last rebuild, Chris Grier had no issues spending free agent money.  After the 2019 “tank” season, he spent over $236M in contracts the following year.  That didn’t go well, but then he had another spending spree in 2022 with a HC change and that one did work out with several players, such as Terron Armstead, Raheem Mostert, and Connor Williams. Green Bay on the other hand has used free agency sparingly with mixed results. They signed safety Xavier McKinney and RB Josh Jacobs to big deals in 2024 and those additions were successes. In 2025, they signed OG Aaron Banks and CB Nate Hobbs to big deals in 2025 and those additions were not so successful. Sully will have the cap space to operate and get free agents, but don’t expect a massive overhaul and all the big names; figure one or two guys at most. The rest will be cheap players who are chasing the carrot. This is how he will run things.

The issue with free agency in 2027 is where Miami’s areas of need intersect with available talent.  Spotrac has a list of players expected to be available in the 2027 offseason.  There aren’t any special talents available that fit the needs of younger players and game changing talent.  I linked two groups: edge rusher and offensive tackle.  There are two names of interest to me in the edge group: Kayvon Thibodeaux and Kingsley Enagbare.  Both are young players that could help the Dolphins and Enagbare comes from the Packers pipeline.  But aside from those two, there is nothing there that makes you want to get excited at either position group. I’m sure someone else will shake free, but those are usually older players that are making too much or whatever. That’s not what Miami is looking to do. They want building blocks. Do you see any in free agency?

That leads to the second issue which is draft need and the quarterback position.  So far, Malik Willis hasn’t answered enough questions to prove he’s the one.  There is still time for him this season, but it’s clear now that the Dolphins are not getting many, if any wins.  Even if he does play great.  If the Dolphins do make the choice to draft a quarterback with their 1st round pick, that sets into motion a draft scenario where now they are looking for skill talent or perhaps another OL starting in round 2.  Miami’s round two pick will be high also, but Barry Jackson highlighted the concerns of this in a recent article.  The Dolphins will have to hope that Sully has another run of good picks later, otherwise they have started spinning their wheels.  In other words, if pick 1 is a QB, then the Dolphins will be relying on later picks to fill positions of need.  That slows down the process unless Sully has atypical draft results.

The final issue goes back to the tweet from ct.  What if the Dolphins go 0-17 and there is a coaching change?  That compounds the other two issues because now there is more change to go along with a younger and incomplete roster.  When the coaching change happened in 2022, Miami already had some pieces in place PLUS a roster that had been winning.  The transition was a little easier.  If Hafley becomes a one-and-done HC, then any potential positives that have been build this season could be swept away in the switch i.e. the players that Hafley likes may not be players the new HC likes.  One of the comments from last week was disappointed by the HC talk, but I only bring it back up because, well… I’m not the only one thinking it.

I write all of this to say that extreme patience will be the biggest need for this fanbase.  There are already people disgusted by the outcomes and wanna change this or that.  That’s a little extreme at this stage, but it highlights an underlying viewpoint that I’m afraid will catch many fans off-guard in 2027.  And that is there will not be a 5-12 to 10-6 turnaround like from 2019 to 2020.  This is going to be 0-17/1-16/2-15 to 4-13/5-12/6-11 type of turnaround.  Then MAYBE they get to 9-10 wins in 2028 and then be true contenders in 2029.  I made that assertion in the offseason and I’m sticking to that.  I haven’t seen anything from this team, particularly from this quarterback and HC combo that would make me feel any different.  There is a LONG way to go. I said pre-draft that drafting a guard at 11 would slow the rebuild down and some said I couldn’t link causation of those two things.  Perhaps not, but maybe it was a covert indication that Sully already knew this would take several years.  Settle in folks… we’re going to be here for a while.

item.title: Cowboys offense provides fireworks while the defense is still a little leaky
item.description: Last week was a step in the right direction.
item.content:encoded:
Divisional games are always a battle, so watching the Dallas Cowboys come away with a 37-20 win over the Washington Commanders should feel good, even if it was a little ugly at times. The Cowboys needed a good rebound game after a shaky performance last week, and they got it. Bravo?

Even with the win, it’s hard to know how we should feel about this game, so today we’re going to look closer at things to get a better sense of how this group played. Let’s run through some things that stood out on Sunday.

Prescott was dealing

The passing game was great thanks to Dak Prescott. He finished 26 of 31 for 279 yards with four touchdowns and no picks. He finished with a passer rating of 143.7, his highest mark since the regular-season finale trouncing of the Eagles back in 2022.

The great thing about Prescott’s play is he had some easy stuff drawn up for him with some nifty play designs to get receivers open, but he also made some difficult, spot-on throws to receivers in tighter coverage.

He also made good decisions with his feet, running at the right moments, although it still made fans hold their breath considering how many quarterbacks were getting hurt across the league on Sunday.

Prescott was dialed in, spreading the ball around and making all the right decisions. It was great to see, and it was only fitting that this performance allowed him to pass Tony Romo for the all-time record in passing touchdowns in franchise history. Well done, QB1.

Running game troubles

The only blemish in an otherwise great performance from the offense was their inability to run the ball. Javonte Williams never got anything started as he was met in the backfield on what felt like every other play. The interior offensive line could not get any push, and you cannot help but wonder how much they are missing Tyler Smith, who continues to miss games while recovering from thumb surgery.

Adding to the issue is that they routinely forgot to block the edge defender. Washington repeatedly snuck in extra run attackers along the edge, and the Cowboys left those guys unattended, allowing them to crash in and blow up the run behind the line of scrimmage.

Give the Commanders credit. They were strong in the trenches, particularly Javon Kinlaw. The veteran defensive tackle consistently won at the point of attack, moving blockers and shutting down running lanes. And safety Nick Cross was an effective run-blitzer. There just wasn’t much room for runners to run.

The only good thing about the lack of a rushing attack is that Brian Schottenheimer opted to move away from it rather than continuing to run negative plays. That doesn’t make the problem go away, but it is a nice mitigation tactic, so give him credit for adjusting. The bootlegs and play-action were plenty effective with the Commanders always so focused on attacking the run. The offense kept throwing the ball despite the game script practically screaming at them to run it.

Quietly doing his job

The run-blocking needs serious work, but the pass-blocking is holding up well. Specifically, Tyler Guyton is quietly putting together a great start to the season. He was the subject of endless scrutiny this summer to the point where he was supposedly in a roster battle for his job, but he has since silenced any doubters. He did a great job in his pass protection assignments, allowing Prescott a clean, comfortable pocket to operate from.

Not every first-round lineman the team drafts turns into an immediate All-Pro, but Guyton’s progress is super encouraging. He could still be on that path, even if his route is turning out to be a little more scenic.

Thank goodness for DB depth

It was just a few weeks ago when we couldn’t determine which safeties were going to make final roster cuts because the team was so deep with talent. Fortunately, the front office hung on to that depth, because it did not take long for them to need every single bit of it.

They were already playing without starting free safety Malik Hooker, who suffered a fractured forearm in the opener last week. His replacement, P.J. Locke, only lasted three plays before suffering a non-contact foot injury. Fortunately, the defense still had rookie Caleb Downs, free agent Jalen Thompson, and special teams sub Markquese Bell to hold things down. Downs had a few moments where he made rookie mistakes, but he gets splashier and splashier with each new game.

Additionally, starting cornerback Cobie Durant suffered a hamstring injury, forcing the team to call upon second-year player Shavon Revel Jr. to fill the void. While the young cornerback still has some moments to clean up, he also did a great job riding receivers toward the sideline. Three times in this game he used the boundary perfectly, and all three instances resulted in incompletions.

Linebacker play

The team was also without starter DeMarvion Overshown, who injured his hamstring last week. This put more of the workload on rookie Jaishawn Barham and new acquisition Dee Winters. There were moments where Barham looked a bit overaggressive and overran the play, or Winters was stiff-armed out of the play, but there were also times where both stepped up and shut things down. Ultimately, they combined on the biggest defensive play of the afternoon when Barham forced a fumble, and Winters pounced on it.

Weakness or tightening?

You can easily paint a narrative that the defense was still allowing opposing offenses to march down the field at will. In seven of the Commanders’ nine possessions, they moved the ball to the Dallas 36-yard line or better. That is a lot of chances to give up points, and Washington racked up almost 400 yards of offense.

But you can also make a strong case that the defense tightened up when it mattered. Washington only managed to score two touchdowns. There were two clear scoring opportunities where the Commanders walked away with absolutely zero points. Granted they had some self-inflicted mishaps that hurt their chances, but the Cowboys didn’t let them off the hook.

People will point to that unfortunate incident on the last play of the first half, but don’t forget the two plays before that. Washington had chances to punch the ball in from the one-yard line, but the defense forced two straight incompletions from Jayden Daniels.

The defense also forced a three-and-out to open the game and a quick turnover midway through the third quarter that completely changed the momentum. These are good things that the defense deserves credit for.

QB containment is still a thing

The defense struggled mightily to bring the quarterback down. The pressure was inconsistent, sometimes getting close, other times allowing the quarterback to have all day. In every instance, they could never quite finish the play with a sack.

Even knowing it is a strength of Washington’s offense, the front seven failed to keep the quarterback in the pocket. The QB kept eluding defenders and churning out big gains on the ground. Watching the game closely, there were some instances where Daniels was very decisive and very fast, and sometimes you have to just recognize the other team has great players too, so it wasn’t as egregious as it initially appeared. It’s still something to be mindful of.

While last week the defense was burned by designed runs, on Sunday it came from pure improvisation because the defense was not equipped to make stops in space. The good news is the team will be moving to a stretch of games against quarterbacks with far less mobility soon. The bad news is they have Lamar Jackson coming up next, so it might get a little worse before it gets better.

Special teams shout-out

We always talk about the special teams when they do poorly, so it is only fair that we give them props when they show out. Brandon Aubrey was fantastic. Yes, he did have that one squib kick that fell short of the landing zone, which gave Washington great field position, but he also had a few others that the returner struggled to handle cleanly. Honestly, it is impressive what he is doing, and it would not surprise me if one of those squibbers produces a turnover at some point.

Aubrey also casually nailed a 60-yarder. No big deal. He knocked it down like it was an extra point. Replay showed the ball hitting the back of the net, meaning that one had the distance to break the NFL record. It is only a matter of time before he does that. We all know it is coming.

It was not just Aubrey doing all the heavy lifting either. KaVontae Turpin deserves a lot of credit for constantly making good returns. He consistently got past the first line of defense and brought the ball out past the 30-yard line, and he came close a couple of times to taking one to the house.

The coverage team was sharp too. With the aid of some good kicks, the special teams unit attacked quickly, and who didn’t love that thunderous hit from Brevyn Spann-Ford? It was a great performance by the special teams group.

This game showed that the team has the offensive explosive firepower to mask its defensive flaws, at least for now. The schedule will get tougher. Prescott is playing with that MVP-type vibe, so that is exciting.

While the defense is taking its share of punches, it held up a little better this time around. There are still things to improve on both sides of the ball, but this was a good momentum-building win. If they can just fix a few things, the outlook for the season will improve.

item.title: The Day After the Day After: Reliving the Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals
item.description: Another home game against a contender. Another loss. Sigh...let's get this over with
item.content:encoded:
The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 2:

Houston’s D-Line was Good; Cincinnati’s was Better: The Texans generated 5 sacks, held the Bengals to 80 yards total rushing and made the Bengals work for everything. Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter upped their play. Yet, it was the Bengals’ D-Line that ruled the game. They held Houston to only 60 total yards rushing, with RBs Marks and Montgomery only managing 18 combined. They obliterated the Houston interior, and it was all Stroud could do to keep out of their way until the 4th Quarter, when the Bengals sacked him four times. They surrendered over 350 yards in the air, but only 6 points. Dexter Lawrence took whatever Texans’ interior player he faced and made them into a glorified blocking dummy. How dominant was that Bengals’ interior? Houston only attempted four designed running plays in the 2nd half. 

0-4: Box Scores aren’t the end-all/be-all for a game. They can’t always tell the full story. However, there are times when they can say everything. If you had not watched the game and just went to the box score to see how this game played out, you would find this for Houston: 

  • 4th Down Conversions: 0/4
  • Red Zone (Attempts/Makes): 0/4

Last season, a big reason why the team struggled to that 0-3 and 3-5 start was that the offense could not convert on 3rd/4th Down and they couldn’t convert in the Red Zone. Houston was 5 of 17 on 3rd Down, so they were already in pain there. Yet, to go 0 for 4 on a follow-up 4th Down…not good at all. This included the 4th and 4 at the CIN 16 when the muffed FG snap happened; a 4th and 1 at the CIN 16, resulting in a stuff by Dexter Lawrence; a 4th and 1 at the HOU 41 in the 4th Quarter resulting in an incomplete pass; a 4th and 17 sack at the CIN 19 that ended the game for Houston. Just a critical in those data points, three of the four 4th Down conversion failures happened in the CIN Red Zone. 4 total trips into the CIN Red Zone with ZERO points scored. For reference, the Bengals only got into the Red Zone once, but they made it count with a TD pass to Chase in the 3rd Quarter. 

Special Teams…Yikes!!!: This was a game to forget for that unit. Fairbairn went 2-for-3, including missing a 58-yarder, which he can normally make. P Kai Kroeger’ punting was solid for the most part, but his most notable play was a botched snap in the 2nd quarter, which deprived Houston of a key scoring opportunity. The coverage units for punts and kickoffs were not all that impressive, and a critical 15-yard penalty after a 15-yard punt return by the Bengals early in the 3rd quarter set up a Bengals’ scoring opportunity.  The Kroeger muff was not helped by a less-than-ideal snap from Austin Brinkman. As a long-time Texans fan, one thing that is not a common occurrence is a bad kicking snap/hold. 

The Critical Plays: 

  • 2nd Quarter (6:58): 4th and 1 at the CIN 16: David Montgomery -1 yard rush (Dexter Lawrence on the stop)
  • 3rd Quarter (5:56): 3rd and 7 at the HOU 49: Joe Burrow pass to Samaje Perine for 16 yards (HOU 33)

There were two critical conversion plays in this game. Both went against Houston. The first one not only dented a Houston drive, but it seemed to alter the decision-making process of the Texans. The running game struggled even before that stuff, but it seemed to confirm to Houston that they were not going to get much of anything on the ground. You wouldn’t think that much could scare Ryans, but that play did. In the third quarter, Houston faced another potential 4th and 1, but at the CIN 40. After two failed plays before, and remembering what happened in the 2nd Quarter, Ryans settled for a 58-yard FG attempt. It failed, and it set up the next situation.

The second play saw Houston only down 7 (10-3). After the missed FG, the Bengals got the ball in good field position, but faced 3rd and 7 at the HOU 49. If the defense gets the stop, the Bengals likely punt and Houston gets the ball back. The Houston D-line forced Burrow to move around in the pocket. However, the secondary coverage could not hold and Burrow found his Perine to catch and run for 16 yards to the HOU 33. That conversion kept the Bengals’ drive alive, culminating in a 18-yard TD pass to Ja’Maar Chase. At 17-3, and with the running game M.I.A., this made Houston one-dimensional, and against the Bengals’ D-Line on this day, that did not bode well. 

FUN WITH NUMBERS: 

2-6: Houston Texans’ record in regular season games under Ryans in the Summer: Perhaps Ryans and the Texans take it literally that the NFL is a fall sport and that the games don’t really start until after the Equinox. The one exception was 2024, when Houston actually went 2-0 in Summer games. 

6:Total number of sacks surrendered by Houston in the 4th Quarter this season: Houston has given up 7 sacks this season. All but one happened in the 4th quarter. The two on the final three plays against Buffalo, and then in this game, when the Bengals had no reason to worry about the Texans’ run game and Stroud was forced to make all of the plays with his arm, all four of the Bengals’ sacks came at that time.

37.5%:Conversion percentage for Houston’s offense when facing 3 yards or less: Houston faced 8 total plays needing 3 yards or less to convert for a 1st down. They only converted on 3 of those. On plays where Houston only needed 1 yard to convert: 16.7%. 

GAME BALLS 

DE Will Anderson, Jr: He was back to his usual relentless self, abusing the Bengals with 8 total tackles (4 solo)/1.0 sack/3.0 TFLs/2 QB hits/1 PD. On his credited sack, he was effectively embraced by the tackle, but it made no difference. Anderson also set up another sack by Hall, as he bulled all the way to Burrow, grabbing his foot and allowing Hall to clean-up. 

TE Dalton Schultz: No Nico Collins hurt, especially in the Red Zone. However, Stroud had a dependable backup security blanket in Schultz. 12 receptions for 140 yards will do that.

SHOULD BE FORCED TO EAT ONLY SKYLINE CHILI, WITH BEANS AND STALE SPAGHETTI, FOR THE REST OF THE FALL SEASON

Texans’ Interior O-line players: The whole of the O-line could live here, especially in the 4th quarter, but the interior was completely overwhelmed by the Bengals’ D-Line. Houston could not stop Lawrence and many times Stroud had to roll out of the pocket or could not step into his throws as the center was collapsing too quickly.  

Officials’ UCLs: 21 total flags between both teams. For Cincinnati, their 12 penalties did a lot to keep Houston in this matchup. Not that Houston was playing that much cleaner, as they lost more yards in penalties (83 to CIN’s 78).

Houston’s Sporting Teams: You know about the Texans, but they weren’t alone. It started Friday night when the Houston Cougars went up to rival Texas Tech and couldn’t hold a double-digit lead. The Astros entered the weekend with a one-game lead in the AL West. They left down one.  The Houston Dynamo didn’t technically lose but blew a 2-goal second period lead to end up with a tie. At least the Dash won, but they live at the bottom part of the table. 

Houston, now 0-2, will go on the road to take on their division rival, and fellow 0-2 squad, Indianapolis in what is shaping up to be a near-must win for both. Kickoff is slated for noon CDT on CBS/Paramount+

item.title: Are the Saints contenders after beating the Ravens?
item.description: New Orleans just pulled off one of the more impressive wins we’ve seen in a while, but are they legitimate contenders?
item.content:encoded:
It’s time to start taking the New Orleans Saints a little more seriously.

That might sound like an overreaction after just two games, but beating the Baltimore Ravens on the road is the kind of win that gets a team’s attention.

The Saints entered Baltimore as underdogs and found themselves trailing 14-3 in the second quarter. Instead of folding, New Orleans completely flipped the game after halftime, scoring the final 15 points to secure a 24-17 victory.

Tyler Shough continues to show why there is growing excitement surrounding him as one of the NFL’s next star quarterbacks. He completed 27 of 34 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 23 yards on nine carries and the game-winning score with under two minutes remaining. Chris Olave added eight catches for 86 yards and a touchdown, while the defense held Lamar Jackson and the Ravens to only three points after halftime.

Those are the types of complementary performances that can make a team dangerous.

But this is where the overreaction comes in.

The Saints are just two games in, and one road victory doesn’t suddenly erase every question surrounding a team that is still figuring itself out. New Orleans also trailed by double digits for the second consecutive week, meaning the team has plenty to clean up despite its ability to respond.

Still, there is something different about beating a team like Baltimore in its own building.

The Saints now return home for their first game at Caesars Superdome against the 2-0 Las Vegas Raiders. If they can carry the momentum from Baltimore into that matchup, the conversation around this team could change quickly.

Are the Saints contenders?

It is probably too early to say.

But after Sunday, it is no longer unreasonable to ask the question.

item.title: AP Chiefs Mailbag: Will the real Kansas City defense please stand up?
item.description: Arrowhead Pride staff writer Jared Sapp answers your questions about Kansas City after a close win in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag!Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs!

It took a full 70 minutes, but the Chiefs are 2-0 thanks to a 33-30 overtime victory over the Indianapolis Colts Sunday night. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds ahead of a trip to South Florida to face the Miami Dolphins in Week 3.

MrAustin.Sr asks:


Which defense is REALLY our defense, last week vs the Denver Broncos or the defense we ran out there for the Colts?

This will sound like a cop out, but the answer is probably somewhere in between. I think there are some context factors we should consider.

The Chiefs had probably been working on the Broncos game plan since midway through training camp. Also, Week 1 was defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s fifth opportunity to game plan against the Denver quarterback Bo Nix’s offense. He clearly made adjustments to keep Denver from repeating some of their success in the pair of 2025 matchups.

Many laughed off the Colts after being blown out by the Baltimore Ravens in Week 1. However, Indianapolis was also among the league’s best offenses in the first half of last season. Indianapolis started 8-2 while averaging 32 points per game. Yes, the wheels fell off down the stretch, but the Colts have definitely shown the ability to score big early.

My biggest concern coming out of the Broncos win was how the defense would react to a team that doesn’t abandon the run early, as Denver did. Hopefully, the team sees some areas to address because it did not go well. The combination of star running back Jonathan Taylor and the Colts’ offensive line is likely a challenge few opponents can replicate.

The biggest issue for the Chiefs’ defense is how long the unit can afford to continue a heavy workload for cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who surrendered a passer rating of 132.6 when targeted in Week 2. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones treated Sneed like an “easy button,” and the Chiefs’ pass rush had little to do to be effective.

Like most things early on, we will need a larger sample. If the Chiefs struggle with the Dolphins — who have surrendered nine sacks through two games and needed a garbage-time touchdown to reach 13 points on Sunday — it will be more concerning.

Will007 asks:


Is it time to start worrying about the wide receivers room or is just the first two games the Chiefs played two teams with good secondaries?

There are two possibilities to ponder with the wideouts. For many, the question is whether the Chiefs have someone in-house who can be a no-doubt No. 1 passing game option. That answer is undoubtedly no.

A different assessment is whether the Chiefs have the potential to replicate the 2022 receiving corps featuring complementary pieces that propelled quarterback Patrick Mahomes to an MVP season. That one is probably a “maybe.”

Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton and Jalen Royals combined for 200 receiving yards and a pair of touchdowns against Indianapolis. To be fair, 31 of those yards came to Rice on the final play of regulation that never had any chance of proving fruitful. But the Chiefs’ receivers did show signs of the “sum of the parts” approach that has worked well in prior seasons.

While you cannot expect tight end Travis Kelce or running back Kenneth Walker to keep up their early-season pace, they are crucial to the Chiefs succeeding with an underwhelming group of wideouts.

Which player gets targets will likely change weekly depending on the opponent. Second-year man Jalen Royals entered the night widely forgotten. Royals only saw two targets, but both came in key situations, and the coaches clearly saw something in the Colts’ defense they felt he could exploit.

Whenever rookie Cyrus Allen’s turn finally comes, it will probably be a similar development.

Andyreidsmustache_ asks:


Has the coaching staff finally seen enough from Tyquan Thornton to actually make him a more prominent part of the offense, if not an outright starter? I’d already put him head and shoulders above Worthy at minimum.

I think the Kansas City wideout group is so matchup dependent that I am rarely concerned with who is nominally starting. I do think Sunday previewed what can be done with Thornton. His 86 receiving yards in Week 2 were more than a tenth of his career production over his first four seasons.

Thornton has never shown the yards-after-the-catch elusiveness to have the value in the short passing game that the other wideouts bring. However, he is easily the Chiefs’ most dependable deep threat since Tyreek Hill left after 2021. As Walker demands more defensive focus, Thornton should find more deep opportunities as he did on Sunday night.

Worthy’s start to the season has been frustrating, but I still think it is early to write off his season. Remember that over three years with the New England Patriots, Thornton definitely looked like the far inferior player.

RoyalsFanBill asks:


Who is our primary kick returner going forward?

The Chiefs seem to be trying to make running back Brashard Smith the focused returner. Rookie Emmett Johnson took one kickoff Sunday night. While both appear to have more juice than Remigio, I would be wary of using both backup running backs as the return tandem because of the risk of having both options behind Walker injured at the same time.

Perhaps the Chiefs are seeing that Remigio’s speed limitations lead to penalties because it takes him longer to reach his blockers. Hopefully, Smith will get more opportunities on punts and kickoffs as the season goes on.

FoxBot2021 asks


Will AP ever just be happy the team wins? Or will everything always be nitpicked because people wamt a “perfect victory”?

A long time ago — in a Chiefs Kingdom that seems far, far away — I watched the 2002 squad steal a Week 1 victory because Cleveland Browns linebacker Dwayne Rudd threw his helmet in celebration before time expired and drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. An untimed down allowed a 30-yard game-winning field goal.

When I see the current state of social media during Chiefs games, I wonder if we would even feel permitted to celebrate that moment if it happened today. My opinion is that now multiple generations have grown up playing Madden and believe that anything short of a three-touchdown margin of victory doesn’t truly count as a win.

The truth is, the NFL is a tough business, and the margin between perceived good and bad teams is rarely as wide as fans believe. Players know how short their careers can be, and you should expect every team’s best shot every week. The first month of the season is increasingly unpredictable as teams enter the campaign with less preseason action than in previous generations. Several teams that entered 2026 with lofty expectations would have taken a tight overtime victory over how their own Week 2 contests went.

Eight squads are 2-0, and the Chiefs are one of them. It would be naive to think there aren’t areas for improvement. But sometimes a game turns out closer than expected — and it’s ok just to be happy with the win.

Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with a road game in Miami on Sunday. Keep watchingThe Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

item.title: Why we shouldn’t be surprised Greg Rousseau is making the leap in Year 6
item.description: Rousseau looks to be hitting his stride as a professional this season
item.content:encoded:
Greg Rousseau is becoming a huge win for age-related draft analysis.

Even after sitting out his second season at the University of Miami due to COVID, the Buffalo Bills selected Rousseau with one of the final picks in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft just a few weeks after his 21st birthday.

He was one of the youngest players in that draft, and surprisingly was able to shoulder a full-time workload as a rookie at defensive end.

Since then, he’s been a steady yet mostly unspectacular edge rusher in Buffalo. His regular-season pressure rate has hovered between 14.0% and 14.9%. Quite impressive, really.

That is until the first two games of 2026 within Jim Leonhard’s scheme. Rousseau’s pressure rate is a massive 23.1% entering Week 3, and he already has four sacks on the year, matching his rookie-year total and just one shy of the five he accumulated as a 23-year-old in 2023.

Just 26 years old, Rousseau has probably just entered the the prime of his career, and he’s already played 3,507 snaps — counting playoffs — in his NFL career. Along the way, he’s learned a variety of ways to collapse the pocket, work around tackles, and track the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.

Like on his first sack of the season, a strip-sack of C.J. Stroud in the first quarter of opening weekend against the Texans, watch how he swiped away the chipping tight end, then worked back to the inside as he felt the quarterback stepping into the pocket.

Textbook. The clean, around-the-corner wins are flashy. The big-time sack producers understand how to follow the quarterback as he glides around in the pocket.

The game-sealing sack late in the fourth quarter was a tremendous display of his maturity rushing the quarterback. Against the impossibly large and lengthy Trent Brown, Rousseau used an inside-arm stab before climbing around Brown’s outside shoulder before getting his right arm on the football as Stroud unsuccessfully attempted to evade the rush again.

That play was a fine example of why length matters along the defensive line. Not only to establish first contact at the point of attack… but to have the reach to get your hands on the football once you enter the pocket.

Right when Rousseau has the offensive tackles thinking he’s a lanky-ish, finesse rusher… he can deploy a nasty straight-arm bull rush, like he did hear against the typically serviceable swing tackle Larry Borom.

His second sack against the Lions was the byproduct of bad offensive schematics from the Lions — as Rousseau was left with a tight end on him in pass pro.

Obviously, Rousseau quickly worked through the tight end and forced another fumble on a sack.

Referencing yesterday’s article on Buffalo’s pass rush converting pressures to sacks at a much higher clip than at any stage of the Sean McDermott era, Rousseau is a key aspect of that.

Rousseau entered this season with a career 14.6% pressure-to-sack rate himself, and only in 2023 was that single-season rate higher than 15% — it was 21.4%.

Thus far in the 2026 campaign, Rousseau has four sacks on 16 pressures, good for a 25% pressure-to-sack rate in Leonhard’s new scheme.

And check where he is in the Pass-Rush Win Rates as compiled by PFF and SumerSports.

By year No. 6 in the NFL, we almost always know precisely who a player is.

But at his age, Rousseau has ample experience and really is entering the peak physical timeframe of his professional career. And, this season, he looks well on his way to realizing all the upside that was a key element of his draft profile all the way back in 2021.

item.title: Dan Campbell can’t reassure fans who think Kerby Joseph’s career is done
item.description: Is Kerby Joseph’s career over? Detroit Lions coach Dan Cambpell couldn’t say.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell noted that safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph will remain sidelined on the Physically Unable to Perform list, despite them being eligible to return to practice this week. He noted that Branch is closer to returning than Joseph, and then gave some additional details on Joseph’s recovery from a knee injury that has now lingered for over a full year.

“We were strengthening the knee, and it wasn’t a setback, but there was a little time there where we weren’t able to do everything we needed to do. And so now we’re back at it,” Campbell said. “And until we can get the knee to a certain point to where it feels strong, as strong as we can possibly get it and he feels comfortable. We’re not going to put him out there until he’s ready.”

Lions fans have been understandably skeptical about Joseph’s football future. The team has said there is no surgery or procedure that fixes this issue. It’s something Joseph will just have to manage. At times, it seems like the former All-Pro safety was nearing a return, only for Campbell to provide a dubious update.

So some have started to question whether Joseph will ever play another down of football in his life.

On Tuesday, 97.1 The Ticket radio host Jim Costa asked Campbell what he would say to Lions fans who think Joseph will never play again. Campbell’s response was not reassuring.

“Well, I wish I could make you feel good. I can’t make you feel good,” Campbell said. “It’s going to come as it comes, and he’s not ready. We’re trying to get him there as fast as we can, and we’re trying to be as smart about it as we can. And if he’s ready, when he’s ready, of course we want to play him and get him on the field.”

Costa followed it up with another question, and Campbell gave a puzzling response that did not sound particularly good:

Costa: “What would have to change? Because we’re coming up on a year since that Chiefs game. If he’s unable to practice what would change for him to get out there?”

Campbell: “I guess, nothing.“

At this point, it certainly seems like the Lions are operating under the assumption they are going to get very little—if anything—out of Joseph this season. And you have to wonder what that means for the rest of his football career with a $16.6 million option bonus due in March of 2027.

item.title: My 5 Rams’ game balls from MNF victory over Giants
item.description: 5 game ball recipients from Rams MNF win over the Giants
item.content:encoded:
Sean McVay has never been shy about handing out a game ball(s) after a victory. After all, a win is never to be taken for granted.

The Los Angeles Rams defeated the New York Giants 28-6 in a great team effort win. There were still flaws and some areas of execution that need to be cleaned up but overall it was a solid bounce back performance by the preseason favorites. Who helped steer the team to victory and shined under the Monday Night Football lights? Here are MY game balls from the team’s Week 2 win…

Game Ball #1: Davante Adams

Without hesitation, Adam was the biggest performer of the night. His 8 receptions for 195 yards and 2 touchdowns paced the Rams. His 195 yards also outgained the New York Giants entire offense. Adams looked like the Green Bay Packer version of himself. Something the Rams were hoping to resurrect when they signed him last offseason. With Puka Nacua sidelined, Adams big night carried even more significance on the field and in the stat sheet.

Game Ball #2: Matthew Stafford

Stafford looked like the 2025 MVP Stafford. He threw for 327 yards, 4 touchdowns, and 1 interception. The interception in the 2nd quarter was reckless and overambitious but that is what you will get with Stafford sometimes. But all in all, Stafford was methodical, sharp, and in-sync throughout the majority of the night. Terrance Ferguson actually dropped two passes which hurt Stafford’s completion percentage.

Game Ball #3: Kobie Turner

I thought Kobie Turner was a force for the defense. I was worried about how the Rams defensive line would handle Cam Skattebo but Turner led the charge in slowing down the powerful back. There may not have been any splash plays but Turner showed up on the tape.

Game Ball #4: Sean McVay

Sure the HC is not going to get the game ball typically but McVay was pretty flawless in his play calling. The only blemishes in the game were player-inflicted. Matthew Stafford’s interception. Kyren Williams fumble. Harrison Mevis’s missed field goal. Terrance Ferguson’s two drops. McVay himself called a great game. And his team responded the way they needed to after an opening Week 1 loss.

Game Ball #5: Trent McDuffie

The Rams traded a first round pick and paid Trent McDuffie to be the highest paid cornerback in the league. Well against Malik Nabers, the star cornerback held the talented wide receiver to 1 reception for 1 yard on 4 targets. McDuffie also got his hands on his first interception as a Ram. #22 also added a key PBU on a deep ball pass attempt to Nabers in the 2nd quarter.

It appeared the Rams shifted to more man-coverage in the game and McDuffie put his skill set on display; earning himself plenty of praise for the MNF performance.

item.title: 49ers’ upcoming stretch will test Trent Williams’ exciting Brock Purdy claim
item.description: Even though his latest superb showing came against significantly inferior opposition in the form of the Miami Dolphins, the excitement around what 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy has put together through the opening two weeks of the season is understandable. Purdy was near-perfect in the 49ers’ 35-13 rout of the rebuilding Dolphins, rewriting several pages of […]
item.content:encoded:
Even though his latest superb showing came against significantly inferior opposition in the form of the Miami Dolphins, the excitement around what 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy has put together through the opening two weeks of the season is understandable.

Purdy was near-perfect in the 49ers’ 35-13 rout of the rebuilding Dolphins, rewriting several pages of the record books in going 20 of 22 for 287 yards and two touchdowns. Purdy also led the 49ers in rushing with 30 yards and a rushing score.

Those numbers saw Purdy become the first player in NFL history to complete at least 90 percent of his passes, throw for at least 285 yards and two touchdowns and rush for a score in the same game.

With a completion percentage of 90.9, Purdy now owns the top two single-game completion percentage marks in 49er franchise history. He completed 95.2% of his passes against the Arizona Cardinals in a 35-16 win in October, 2023. In addition, he joined Derek Carr as only the second player to have multiple games with a completion rate of 90%-or-higher and at least 250 passing yards.

His passer rating of 149.1 gave Purdy an eighth career game with a rating of 140-or-higher and a 13th game with a rating of at least 130-or higher, both NFL records for a player in the first five seasons of his career.

Unsurprisingly, the praise for Purdy after the game from his teammates was effusive, though it was the comments of Trent Williams that were the most eye-catching.

Asked what impressed him most about Purdy’s showing, the left tackle said:

“It’s hard for me to tell because I just see the ball coming over my head, but it was extremely accurate. He looked like he was just at practice out there, wheeling and dealing. Like I said, we’re starting to witness Brock’s prime and I think it’s going to be a sight to behold. To me, I’ve always loved Brock, but I think he’s starting to get his respect now. He doesn’t even relish in it. It’s all about next week, going 1-0, and that’s why he’s a great leader.”

Williams’ remarks about Purdy hitting his prime suggest even more impressive games are to come from the 49ers’ signal-caller, but those exciting claims will be severely tested over the coming weeks.

An exacting three-game stretch

San Francisco’s schedule over the next three games is very tough, with the 49ers hosting the Cardinals and the Denver Broncos before making the trip up to the Pacific Northwest for a matchup with the Seattle Seahawks.

While the visit of the Cardinals is not a fixture to inspire much fear, a divisional game against an opponent that has played the 49ers tough in recent years is not be taken lightly, though it is the meetings with the Broncos and Seahawks that will provide the sternest early examinations of Purdy’s progress this year.

Facing a Denver defense that led the NFL in sacks (68) last season promises to be an extremely difficult challenge for Purdy, as does a reunion with a Seattle unit that overwhelmed the 49ers in Week 18 and in the divisonal round last season.

And the severity of the test he will face is potentially exacerbated by the 49ers’ injury issues at wide receiver, where Demarcus Robinson is the latest player to be sidelined, having suffered a high-ankle sprain.

Robinson joining De’Zhaun Stribling and Chirstian Kirk among the injured players at receiver is a huge hit to the 49ers’ depth at wideout and, while San Francisco still has high end weapons in the likes of Christian McCaffrey, Mike Evans and George Kittle, a paucity of supplementary options makes Purdy’s job in overcoming two vaunted defenses that much harder.

The 49ers’ 2025 season ended in ugly fashion with Purdy out of answers against the Seahawks as injuries left San Francisco with a skill-position cast ill-equipped to keep their playoff game competitive. The Niners still have enough weapons to trouble both Denver and Seattle but, with injuries impacting the depth, this upcoming slate and Purdy’s ability to find solutions amid the offense’s injury woes will provide an indicator as to the prescience of Williams’ comments about his quarterback.

item.title: NFC South Week 2 Review: Two impressive wins, two embarrassing losses
item.description: Tampa Bay and Atlanta are quickly falling into the basement of the division.
item.content:encoded:
The Panthers and Saints grab their first wins of the season, while the Falcons and Buccaneers quest for a W continues. The division’s young quarterbacks are making a case that their time is now.

Are the Buccaneers already feeling buyer’s remorse, and will the Falcons ever reach the red zone? Here’s the Week 2 NFC South Review.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-2)

Week 2 Result: Buccaneers 19 – Browns 23

Week 3 Opponent: Minnesota Vikings

The Buccaneers are a volatile product, as they’ve always been during the Bowles-Mayfield era, but things feel different this year. Mayfield has only thrown for one touchdown across two games, and Tampa Bay is 0-2 for the first time since 2024. Bowles’ defense couldn’t hold off a second-half surge from the Browns, and unlike most seasons, Tampa Bay isn’t dealing with a laundry list of injuries.

If this team can’t get a win soon, Todd Bowles could find himself unemployed before the season ends. The Buccaneers will host the 2-0 Vikings, who will have Kyler Murray under center after he cleared concussion protocol Monday.

New Orleans Saints (1-1)

Week 2 Result: Saints 24 – Ravens 17 

Week 3 Opponent: Las Vegas Raiders

The Saints scored 15 unanswered points in the 4th quarter, delivering an upset on the road in Baltimore. Tyler Shough is looking like the quarterback he was hyped up to be all offseason. The offense has shown its potential in the first two weeks, but the defense deserves credit for keeping the Ravens offense in check in the second half.

Chase Young has been off to an impressive start, and if this defense can keep playing complementary football, this team will be a force in the division. The Saints return home to host the red-hot Raiders, who are 2-0. 

Carolina Panthers (1-1)

Week 2 Result: Panthers 34 – Falcons 3

Week 3 Opponent: Detroit Lions

Bryce Young continues to torment the Dirty Birds. He delivered another cerebral performance, escaping pressure with ease and consistently finding the open man. After building a quick lead, the Panthers defense stuffed the Falcons in a locker. Devin Lloyd was all over the field, racking up a sack, two TFLs, two interceptions, and a touchdown.

There is a Cooper Rush/Jack Strand tax applied here, but credit to the Panthers for taking care of a weaker opponent the way a good team should. They’ll host the Lions in Charlotte, who are desperate to turn their 0-2 start around.

Atlanta Falcons (0-2)

Week 2 Result: Falcons 3 – Panthers 34

Week 3 Opponent: Green Bay Packers

The Falcons lost by 30 and were shut out in their first 2025 matchup against the Panthers. This Sunday they lost by 31, but hey, they got on the board this time. This offense is a disaster, and this defense already looks stretched thin after two games. Tommy Rees is struggling, and his offense has more than personnel problems; it’s schematically inept.

Special teams hasn’t looked sharp, and fans have a right to worry that their 41 year old kicker has lost his touch. It’s a short week for the Falcons, who travel to Green Bay Thursday for their first of three consecutive primetime games. Pray for America.

Two weeks isn’t enough time to make concrete proclamations, which is good news for the Falcons and Buccaneers. There’s still plenty of time to recover, but if things don’t get back on track for the 0-2 teams, the Saints and Panthers could make this a two-team race by mid-season.
