item.title: Denver Broncos vs. Jacksonville Jaguars snap counts and analysis
item.description: The Denver Broncos offense ran 62 offensive plays and 59 defensive plays on Sunday in the win over the Jacksonville Jaguars. The inactive players for the game were: Sam Ehlinger, RJ Harvey, Marvin Mims, Kage Casey, Dallon Bentley, Jordan Jackson, and Tyler Onyedim. The only active player who did not get in the game was […]
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos offense ran 62 offensive plays and 59 defensive plays on Sunday in the win over the Jacksonville Jaguars.

The inactive players for the game were: Sam Ehlinger, RJ Harvey, Marvin Mims, Kage Casey, Dallon Bentley, Jordan Jackson, and Tyler Onyedim.

The only active player who did not get in the game was Jarret Stidham.

OFFENSE

Bo Nix played every offensive snap. Quinn Meinerz missed two snaps and Alex Palczewski replaced him. The Broncos used six offensive linemen on two plays and Alex Palczewski was that player. Talanoa Hufanga played as the safety on the three victory formation kneeldowns.

Jonah Coleman, JK Dobbins, and Tyler Badie played 25, 21, and 16 snaps on offense. That is the most equitable running back split I have seen in the years that I have been doing this. Adam Prentice got eight snaps at fullback.

Adam Trautman, Evan Engram, and Nate Adkins played 40, 32, and 23 snaps at tight end. Trautman did not get targetted, despite playing 40 snaps. Nate Adkins had four touches (1 run and 3 catches), to one touch for Evan Engram.

The wide receiver snaps were 45 for Courtland Sutton, 41 for Pat Bryant, 38 for Jaylen Waddle, 13 for Troy Franklin, and 3 for Lil’Jordan Humphrey. Pat Bryant was the primary receiver in week one and he had one target in week two, the same as LJH. Waddle was targetted 10 times and got eight catches on those.

Only two active offensive players did not play on offense, Matt Peart and Alex Forsyth (other than Jarret Stidham).

DEFENSE

Defensively three players took every snap, Hufanga, Patrick Surtain, and Alex Singleton. Riley Moss and Brandon Jones played all but one snap.

At the other starting ILB spot, Justin Strnad played 55 snaps. No other ILB played defensive snaps.

At safety JL Skinner got one snap on defense.

The cornerbacks who have not been mentioned played 40 snaps (Ja’quan McMillian) and 2 snaps (Jahdae Barron). Barron’s lack of playing time is hopefully a function of how good the three CBs in front of him are and not a function of how poor he is developing in his second season.

At outside linebacker Nik Bonitto, Jonah Elliss, Que Robinson, and Dondrea Tillman played 40, 41, 19 , and 18 snaps.

Zach Allen, DJ Jones, Malcolm Roach, Eyioma Uwazurike, and Sai’vion Jones played 48, 25, 34, 27, and 6 snaps. Roach and Robinson combined for the two sacks and for three of the team’s seven QBhits. They also had three of the five TFL that the Bronco D had on Sunday.

SPECIAL TEAMS

The guys who played on 50 percent or more of the special team snaps were Kris Abrams-Draine, Devon Key, Jordan Turner, Karene Reid, and Tycen Anderson. KAD was returning punts in the absence of Mims. Anderson, Key, Skinner, and Turner all had tackles on kick off or punt coverage.

item.title: NFL Week 3 Power Rankings: Contender or Pretender?
item.description: Heading into Week 3, the NFL’s parity is on full display. Here’s how @AaronLemingNFL’s Power Rankings look after Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
Somehow, someway, the 2026 NFL regular season has turned the page on Week 2, and we’re onto Week 3. After an unpredictable opening weekend of football, things started to level out a bit in Week 2. Even so, there’s still plenty to learn over the next few weeks about which teams are for real and who are just off to unsustainable starts. With that in mind, let’s dive into our WCG Week 3 Power Rankings!

1. Buffalo Bills (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

The offense is legit, and even if there are questions about the defense (they’ve given up 31 points in consecutive weeks), it should be enough to keep them as strong Super Bowl contenders all season. Josh Allen looks primed for another MVP run, so assuming the defense can get their sea legs under them at some point soon, they might be the most complete team in the AFC. 

2. Seattle Seahawks (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender 

No Sam Darnold, no problem. Following a close first half, the Seahawks pulled away in the second half, and Jaxson Smith-Njigba showed why he’s one of the best receivers in the game. With Darnold expected back within the next week or two, Seattle appears to be in great shape to defend their title in the coming months. 

3. San Francisco 49ers (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

We knew the 49ers offense would be a problem (in a good way) this season, but their defense rounding into form is a great sign. After all, that’s basically what they were missing for most of last season. San Francisco is on a roll right now and doesn’t appear to be slowing down any time soon. It appears the NFC West is once again going to be the best division in football. 

4. Cincinnati Bengals (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

The defense is legit, and that’s something Bengals fans have been hoping for since their trip to the Super Bowl a few years ago. Keeping quarterback Joe Burrow healthy will be the key to their season, but assuming all goes well on that front, there’s no reason to believe that they can’t contend in the AFC and push for a deep playoff run. 

5. Los Angeles Rams (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

Week 1 overreactions are always abundant, but last week felt like a time when way too many people “gave up” on the Rams far too soon. Granted, the injury to Jaxson Dart drastically altered Monday night’s game, but I’m not sure the Giants would have been able to stop that offense, regardless of who they had at quarterback. The wait for Myles Garrett’s return will be painful, but it was good to see Aaron Donald back on the field. The Rams are just fine. 

6. Philadelphia Eagles (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender 

The Eagles are a vastly talented team, and even if neither win has been convincing (+6 points), they are well-rounded on both sides of the ball. They’ll have a nice test on Monday night against the Bears in Chicago, but with Caleb Williams’ hamstring injury, their path to a win should be much easier facing backup quarterback Tyson Bagent. A 3-0 start would be about as best-case scenario as possible, even if none of their wins have looked overly dominant. 

7. Minnesota Vikings (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender 

Any time a team starts 2-0 within their division over the first two weeks of the season, it’s a great sign for things to come. The offense has some questions, especially at quarterback. Still, assuming Kyler Murray can hit the ground running, they’ve given themselves more than enough of a head start to push for a playoff spot, especially with an elite defense that has blitzed both opponents at close to an 80% rate. 

8. Kansas City Chiefs (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender 

Sunday night was a fun one, and it appears that the Chiefs are all the way back. Despite being just nine months removed from a torn ACL, quarterback Patrick Mahomes is moving well, and it’s clear that he still has one of the best arms in the league. Kansas City’s defense looks considerably better than they did last year, even if they gave up a higher point total than ideal in Week 2. The AFC West is there for the taking, and right now, it feels like the Chiefs are ready to take the crown back. 

9. Baltimore Ravens (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

Week 1’s offensive output was about as impressive a debut as offensive coordinator Declan Doyle could have asked for. Week 2 didn’t go as planned, but they kept it close until the final minutes. There’s no reason to think that the Ravens won’t get back on track in Week 3, and overall, they’ve looked like a much more complete team so far in 2026 under first-year head coach Jesse Minter. 

10. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender 

On the road or not, Sunday’s loss came as somewhat of a surprise to most around the league. The Jaguars had been on such a heater that it started to feel like a win was guaranteed each week. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence wasn’t able to follow up on an impressive Week 1, but Denver has one of the best defenses in the league. The good news is that they are in a very winnable division. The bad news is that they have a tough schedule over the next two months. I’m buying what Liam Coen is selling, no matter what the schedule looks like on paper. 

11. Denver Broncos (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

Things didn’t look good against the Chiefs in Week 1, and the offense hasn’t looked the same with offensive coordinator Davis Webb calling plays. That said, this is still a very good defense, and their past success gives them enough track record to believe that they can grab a Wild Card spot at minimum. They’ll face a tough schedule in the immediate future, but their win against the Jaguars proves that they can beat anyone. 

12. New England Patriots (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender

I won’t discount the Patriots’ remaining strength of schedule, including games against the Jaguars, Bills, and Raiders over their next three. That said, this is a well-rounded team with plenty of offensive firepower and a defense that should keep improving. I won’t believe they are “dead” until I see it, and we are far from that point. 

13. Chicago Bears (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBA (Pending Caleb Williams’ health)

Early reports are that Williams avoided a serious injury, and although he might miss a few weeks, the team hasn’t ruled him out for Week 3’s Monday night matchup against the Eagles. Assuming backup quarterback Tyson Bagent can keep them above water, this should be a Wild Card contender at worst. Staying “alive” over the next two games will be key, and it starts with the Eagles on Monday night at Soldier Field. 

14. Detroit Lions (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

The talent is there, but over two weeks, it’s been a mixed bag. Sure, they’ve put up 31 points in back-to-back games, but the majority of that has been put up through two halves in two games. The offense has plenty of talent, but even when healthy, the offensive line has questions. More importantly, the defense is an issue. They’ve given up back-to-back 30-plus-point games (71 overall), over 900 total yards, and have allowed two big quarterback performances—plenty to be learned in the coming weeks, even with an easy schedule. 

15. Green Bay Packers (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

The Packers’ six-game losing streak is over, but it took overtime and two serious injuries to offensive starters to get it done. All-World edge rusher Micah Parsons *can* return in two games, although he might be pacing for shortly after that. That said, their next two games are very winnable, which would land them at 3-1 heading into a big Week 5 matchup against the Bears. We’ll see how they fare on Thursday against a disastrous Falcons team who will be getting their starting quarterback back. 

16. Dallas Cowboys (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

The Week 1 and Week 2 products for the Cowboys couldn’t have been much different. Although I’m not sold on their defense, it’s clear the offense is going to be top-tier yet again. Despite the Eagles being 2-0, the NFC East feels wide open. If the defense can continue to round into form, this is a high-ceiling team with more than enough talent to make some noise en route to a playoff appearance. 

17. Carolina Panthers (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

There are two NFC South teams coming off the board back-to-back here, and both are in similar spots. The division is bad, which could mean only one team makes the playoffs again. That said, there are two teams that look ready to push for a division title, and one of them is the Panthers. The offense is legit, as is quarterback Bryce Young. If the defense can keep improving (against better competition), their ceiling is much higher than last year. 

19. New Orleans Saints (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

The NFC South is extremely winnable, and quarterback Tyler Shough looks like the real deal. A win on the road against the Ravens feels big, and with any luck, this will allow them to get on a roll. This team is still in the midst of a rebuild, but things are improving fast, and they are in the right division to surprise the league. 

19. New York Giants (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

I’m not ready to rule out the Giants as a playoff contender following their Monday night loss, but Jaxson Dart’s injury will be worth monitoring. Without competent quarterback play, this team isn’t good enough to win games consistently. That said, it’s clear that John Harbaugh has made an impact here, and the arrow is pointing up much more than it would have been a year ago, hence the TBD.

20. Houston Texans (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

On the surface, quarterback C.J. Stroud has looked much closer to his rookie self than what we saw in the playoffs in January. That said, it’s easy to argue that there were a lot of empty yards on Sunday against a Bengals defense that allowed just three points. The bigger issue is that their run game remains unproductive. This team has the talent and isn’t a stranger to slow starts. That said, they’ll need to pick it up soon if they plan on finding their way back to the postseason yet again. 

21. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Replacing Mike Tomlin with Mike McCarthy was already a questionable and very uncharacteristic move, but quarterback Aaron Rodgers looks even worse than last year and still isn’t targeting the middle of the field. This roster has talent, but it’s on the older side, and there’s very little elite about it. Step one is fixing this offense, which has been worse than the numbers show through two weeks. 

22. Indianapolis Colts (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Coming into the season, it was already going to be a hard sell for most people to believe that extending Daniel Jones and giving up multiple first-round picks for Sauce Gardner at last year’s deadline was the smart move. With this regime playing on borrowed time, a 0-2 start wasn’t what they wanted. Clearly, they are a better team than that, but how much better is the question.

23. Las Vegas Raiders (2-0)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: TBD

You couldn’t have scripted a better start to the season for the Raiders. Although I’m not convinced that this is sustainable, we see new “surprise” teams every year. Maybe Las Vegas finally has it figured out with this regime. No matter what you label them through two games, this is a great start for them, and we haven’t even seen Fernando Mendoza yet. 

24. Los Angeles Chargers (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

I’m not sure anyone knows what is going on with the Chargers, but it’s bad. Some believe this is just a slow start, but anyone who has watched them knows there are seriously concerning signs after two games. Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and quarterback Justin Herbert have been complete disasters together. Without a complete 180 soon, Los Angeles will face calls for changes heading into the offseason.

25. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Worst division in football or not, the Buccaneers look like a team that is stuck in the mud without much hope in the immediate future. Even after extending quarterback Baker Mayfield and defensive tackle Vita Vea, starting 0-2 against two not-great teams is nothing short of concerning. Despite the bad start, they are still just a game out of first place, with both losses out of conference. That said, this couldn’t look much worse than it has through two games. 

26. Washington Commanders (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Quarterback Jayden Daniels started to look better against the Cowboys’ defense, but another gruesome left elbow injury has derailed his season for a second straight year. Even if he’s healthy, this doesn’t look like a very good team, and without Daniels under center, it could feel like a repeat of 2025. We’ll see how quickly he can return, but things don’t look good no matter his long-term prognosis. 

27. New York Jets (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

The first two weeks of this season feel a heck of a lot better than they did this time last year. That said, this group still has a ways to go, and that’s A-OK. They are still seeking their long-term answer at quarterback, but the talent around the rest of the roster feels a lot more promising so far than it did all of last year. 

28. Arizona Cardinals (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Beating the Chargers in Week 1 felt like the season opener’s biggest upset. Reality came crashing back down against the Seahawks on Sunday, though. The Chargers are now 0-2, and this group looks more like a mid-rebuild outlook than a surprise team. That’s OK, but also a great example of why you must resist the urge to overreact to Week 1. 

29. Atlanta Falcons (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

The good news is the division is wide open, with the leader at 1-1. Atlanta’s bigger issue is its quarterback situation. Cooper Rush proved to be unplayable, and even with Michael Penix coming back Thursday night, what’s the ceiling there? The Falcons feel like they’re trending in the wrong direction, but better quarterback play could change that outlook. 

30. Tennessee Titans (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Truth be told, the Titans were my “surprise” pick to make the playoffs this year, and barring a Bears-like turnaround, there’s going to be far more questions than answers, especially at quarterback. Cam Ward has not shown much growth, and because of that, they’ll struggle to win many games. It’s gutcheck time for the former No. 1 overall pick.

31. Cleveland Browns (1-1)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Pretender

Although their win on Sunday (considering the delay and where their defense was on the field) was impressive, there’s still far too much wrong with this group to sustain a winning record (or anything close to it) this season. They are trending in the right direction, but this is still another year or two away from looking promising. 

32. Miami Dolphins (0-2)

Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender (for the No. 1 overall pick)

There’s not a whole lot to like about what the Dolphins have put on tape through two games this season. Figuring out if Malik Willis is a long-term answer at quarterback is the primary objective for the season, but man, there’s a lot wrong, and understandably so with a team at the start of a rebuild.

item.title: Marvin Harrison Jr. has gone from can’t-miss prospect to Cardinals’ afterthought
item.description: Marvin Harrison Jr. was too good to be a bust, until he wasn’t
item.content:encoded:
There are things that happen in the NFL Draft that simply don’t surprise you after watching classes unfold over the years. It wasn’t the least bit surprising when Zach Wilson became a bust for the Jets after seeing how he played at BYU against cupcake opponents, knowing that his play wouldn’t translate to the NFL. It came as no shock when Troy Williamson busted in 2005, when his only trait was speed, coupled with hands of stone and no route-running ability.

Marvin Harrison Jr. was different. He fell on the other end of the spectrum. Everything in the pre-draft process made him look like a home run pick, a player with every single trait needed to succeed in the NFL. There was nothing about how he played at Ohio State or looked at the combine that could ever indicate he would struggle in the NFL — and in picking him it seemed like the Cardinals were destined to find their next Larry Fitzgerald.

Three years in and the dream has collapsed. Against the Seahawks on Sunday he didn’t register a single catch, locking his season statistics at a paltry two catches for 44 yards. In addition, he’s being phased out of Mike LaFleur’s offense, as Harrison is being pulled off the field on rushing downs, and getting fewer snaps as Michael Wilson has passed by him as the team’s No. 1 receiver, and now even 31-year-old Kendrick Bourne is being more involved in the offense than Harrison is.

Harrison looks dejected on every down, as if he knows the play won’t involve him before the ball is snapped. Quarterback Jacoby Brissett told the media that he believes teams are running two-high safeties against the Cardinals to take away Harrison’s bread-and-butter post route — but that’s a very generous reading from the QB trying to help out a young player in the media. Truth be told: No opponents are thinking about Marvin Harrison Jr at all, because they don’t need to. Three years in we have the unanimous best wide receiver prospect from the 2024 class, and perhaps the most coveted WR prospect ever and he’s not even worth scheming against.

What’s going wrong with Harrison, and is there any way to save him?

Two major blocks are in Harrison’s way right now, and both appear to be mental. There is none of the explosive first step we saw from him at Ohio State, which indicated that he could get early separation. There’s an inherent laziness with how he’s playing the position right now where he’s slow off the line, then meanders into his cuts. This could be a factor of him knowing the play isn’t drawn up with him as the primary, but it’s cuing in the defense to know they don’t have to worry about No. 18 getting the ball. It’s allowing the corner to sit on his hip, while the safety can ostensibly ignore that he’s on the field at all and look at other targets.

On the rare occasions the ball does come Harrison’s way it almost surprises him. Either he’s shocked that he’s being targeted, or he’s in his head too much about making a play — but either way, it’s resulting in drops. At Ohio State there were lapses in focus, but for the most part Harrison was as sure-handed as you’ll find from a top college receiver. During his limited time in the NFL he isn’t necessarily drop-prone, but he makes bad drops at the worst possible time.

All this combines to create a receiver who simply isn’t reliable. If you’re not getting separation on your routes because you’re playing lazy, and you can’t catch the ball when the play opens up for you — then how is a coach or a QB supposed to trust you with a larger role? Richard Sherman noted this problem on Sunday, and he thinks the Cardinals need to do more to feed Harrison to get him out of this funk. While that might be true, at some point an entire football team can’t be sacrificed to artificially manufacture opportunities for a player who isn’t giving 100 percent. Especially when you have a first-year head coach there’s a standard that needs to be established in building a football culture, and that can’t include giving additional reps and plays to someone simply because of their draft status.

This whole scenario is a mess. Marvin Harrison Jr. is spiraling, and there’s no real way to stop it — not really. At this point, it’s feeling a lot like a QB who needs a change of scenery, moving away from the weight of draft expectations to a team where he can fight for a spot, light that fire under him again, and hopefully get things back on track. Right now none of that can happen in Arizona, because the goals of the Cardinals and Harrison can’t be aligned — not without choosing to abandon the season, feed him at all costs, and forget about trying to win football games. That might be good for one player, but not the entire organization.

item.title: Lions film study: What is killing the offense’s opening drives?
item.description: A film study of the Detroit Lions’ slow offensive starts under Drew Petzing in the first two games
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions defense has been the focal point of criticism after surrendering 30 and 41 points, respectively, in their first two games against the New Orleans Saints and the Buffalo Bills. While, overall, the offense has performed well averaging 31 points per game, there is still plenty left to be desired on that side of the ball.

Head coach Dan Campbell was asked about the slow starts in both of the first games.

“But there again, those things are, we can be so much better than we are right now,” explained Dan Campbell. “And we do. We need more out of our offense. They’ll cover for a lot of things when we clean up some of our issues over there too, collectively.”

It is not hard to rationalize how having an offense that starts strong can cover up some of issues the defense is working to correct. There would have been no better defense against Bills quarterback Josh Allen than having an offense that kept him off the field and dictating a game script for Allen to play from behind rather than comfortably with the whole playbook at his disposal.

But that’s not what happened. And a huge factor being the Lions offense going three-and-out in its opening possession against the Saints and the Bills.

Let’s go through each opening series.

In each of the videos linked I have provided the all-22 video of the three-and-out possessions and then will break down each.

New Orleans, Week 1

First-and-10

12 personnel. Unbalanced two tight ends left. Pre snap motion St Brown into the condensed left tight end side.

The Lions open the season with an identity call: a duo/man blocking scheme into the teeth of the defense for a gain of four. Nothing too special to see here, except remember this formation once the ball is snapped and compare it to the second down play against the Bills later on in this breakdown.

Second-and-6

11 personnel. Condensed set.

On a manageable second down, the Saints sit in a soft zone that Detroit takes what is given. St Brown runs an out at the sticks, but is stopped just a yard short after making the catch.

Third-and-1

13 personnel. I-formation.

This should be an automatic if the Lions want to establish themselves as the gritty, Super Bowl contending team the team has been over the past few seasons.

New Orleans runs a stunt inside that puts pressure on center Juice Scruggs, who was starting his first game in Detroit with the injury to Cade Mays. Shown below, the Saints stunt their 2-technique and 1-technique defensive tackles to the left (yellow), while filling in the play-side A gap with linebacker number 20 (orange).

When you watch the embedded video clip above, you can see how this stunt disrupts Scruggs and the blocking scheme when the 1-technique crosses the face of the center. Scruggs is late to the play-side A gap and does not reach the linebacker who makes the stop short of the first down.

Week 1. First series. Third-and-1. Three-and-out.

Unacceptable.

Buffalo, Week 2

First-and-10

11 personnel. Play action, tight end screen pass to LaPorta on the short side.

I think this is a good call to open the game. In the high-energy environment, this concept breaks two tendencies that would be considered the Lions bread and butter: run the ball and attack the middle of the field in the intermediate pass game.

Off the snap, it was a timely call with the Bills blitzing one of their field-side linebacker, who forces Gibbs to transition his run fake to pass protection rather quickly.

The one player away mistake here, from my perspective, is left guard Ben Bartch. After showing his pass block set and releasing for his screen landmark, he keys the linebacker in zone coverage. Bartch, however, takes an angle straight toward the linebacker where he currently is (red arrow), but should attack where he is going to be. (yellow arrow).

As a result, Bartch has to redirect late while not getting a clean block. LaPorta is forced to adjust back inside closer to the pursuit defenders.

Second-and-8

13 personnel. Unbalanced right, outside zone right.

Drew Petzing pulls out the in vogue three tight end personnel grouping, all to the right, field-side of the formation. Note that at the time the ball is snapped, this is the same formation as the first play against the Saints above, but in 13 personnel instead of 12 plus St Brown motioning into the condensed set. This is all part of making the same things look different, and different things looking the same.

Buffalo aligns unconventionally presnap, and stunts according to the diagram shown in the still image below. The 4i- technique crosses the face of right tackle Larry Borom while the 2i- technique crosses the face of the center in the other direction, creating a lane in the A-B gap for the linebackers to fill and scrap against the zone blocking scheme.

Borom’s first step takes him toward the space the 4i is moving into. That gap is Borom’s assignment and it should have been difficult for the Bills defender to cross his face.

The 4i player (#94, Landon Jackson) wins the rep. Buffalo could run whatever games it wanted to attack the A-B gaps with their stunts, if Borom does not let the 4i cross to the C-gap, then Gibbs would have been given an outside alley outflanking the aggressive defensive scheme. This could have been an explosive run that ultimately went for no gain on the play.

Third-and-8

11 personnel.

The Lions attempt to pass the ball with vertical routes out of a trips set to the field, with the slot wide receiver-3 running an out at the sticks.

In a clear passing situation, the Bills run a twist stunt pass rush, picking left guard Bartch with edge Bradley Chubb, freeing defensive tackle Deone Walker for the pressure and sack.

So what does Dan Campbell think the offense can do to start faster?

“Yeah, it’s a good question. And so much of – there is always this, man, how do you start the game? What do you really want to go in doing? What do you hang your hat on? What do you think you can get the most yards or put you in a manageable third or you’re just living in first, second, first? And do you go in, do you try to run it a little bit more depending on the opponent over there where you’re at? Do you come out and you throw it? And I think it’s just finding that balance of what’s the best way to open up the offense early, right?”

After studying the opening possessions, I think Drew Petzing has done a good job at finding that balance. He has mixed different looks, personnel groups, while also anticipating the defense’s aggression or lack thereof.

Each week, however, its been one player who does not quite execute the details of their assignment, putting an end to the drive before it even gets started.

Moving forward, these issues cannot continue.

The offense is too talented.

item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins’ 2026 season has started with two straight losses by an average of 18 points. First, the team lost to the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 1, then was manhandled by the San Francisco 49ers in Week 2. Heading into Week 3, when they host a rolling Kansas City Chiefs team, the immediate future is a little bleak.

That is what happens when a team undergoes a deliberate and deep rebuild. I’ve been through enough of these restarts, rebuilds, recalibrations or whatever you want to call this thing that the winless Dolphins (0-2) are undergoing, to know that the fact is this is going to hurt for a while…

item.title: Aaron Donald feels the love and soreness after first game back with Rams
item.description: Aaron Donald recorded three tackles, including one that resulted in a loss, in the Rams’ 28-6 victory over the Giants at SoFi Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Aaron Donald wore the biggest smile after the Los Angeles Rams’ 28-6 victory over the New York Giants at SoFi Stadium on Monday, Sept. 21.

Donald made his way out of the tunnel during pregame player introductions to a loud cheer from the stadium crowd, which included members of his family.

The defensive tackle produced three tackles, including one that resulted in a loss.

"I felt the love after I had that tackle for a loss and they were cheering for me," Donald said.

The tackle tied Donald with Lavonte David and Von Miller (177) for fourth on the all-time tackles for loss list.

J.J. Watt is third on the list with 195 tackles, with Calais Campbell (196) in second and Terrell Suggs (202) in first. The NFL officially began holding the record for most career tackles for a loss since 1999.

Donald spent time amongst the fans after his postgame press conference, shaking hands and signing some autographs as fans continued to cheer for him.

One of Donald's biggest takeaways was the need to work on his timing moving forward, admitting he could’ve worked faster to win his 1-on-1 matchups.

"I’m a little sore right now," Donald said. "But it feels good to be back out there and get that first game under my belt. … I’m officially back playing football."

Donald did appear to have a wrap around his right hand during the press conference. When asked about it directly, he again just chalked it up to being sore and playing after just two padded practices.

Coach Sean McVay was thrilled to have one of his starting defenders back on the field and the impact he made beyond the stat sheet.

"His overall energy," McVay said, talking about Donald’s impact on the team. "One of the things is he elicits attention. He brings everybody up around him and I didn't think it was by coincidence that was the energy that we played with.

"... I thought the defensive coaches did a great job of their game plan, but ultimately just elevating situations he's in and people that he's around. That's what the greats do and that's what he does."

Donald and the Rams will be back in action against the Denver Broncos in a nonconference road game on Sunday, Sept, 27.

item.title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: Defense saves the day
item.description: The 2025 Bengals lose that game by two touchdowns.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0 to start the 2026 season. They’re alone atop the AFC North, with the Steelers, Ravens and Browns all sitting at 1-1.

All good news!

It’s hard not to be excited about what we saw from the Bengals in Week 2. Winning on the road in the NFL is difficult, especially against a good team—and the Texans are a good team, regardless of their 0-2 start.

What should be most exciting, though, is how the Bengals won.

The offense sputtered, especially in the first half. At this point, I guess that’s just something we should expect from Joe Burrow and the offense early in the season. Had the 2025 Bengals defense played this game, Cincinnati probably loses 30-20.

But this isn’t the 2025 defense.

Dexter Lawrence showed everyone why he was worth the No. 10 overall selection, and the rebuilt defense kept the Texans out of the end zone for the entire game—in their own stadium. Houston’s only points came on field goals from 37 and 45 yards. When the Texans managed to move the ball into Bengals territory, the defense either forced a turnover on downs or Houston shot itself in the foot.

Here are some observations from the game:

  • Lawrence was incredible against the Texans. In the second quarter, Houston opted to go for it on fourth-and-inches in the red zone. The game was still scoreless, and the Texans passed up the easy points in hopes of picking up a fresh set of downs, getting the crowd into the game and building some momentum before halftime. Lawrence wasn’t having it. He split a double team and tracked down David Montgomery in the backfield, forcing a turnover on downs and giving the ball back to Cincinnati. On the following drive, Burrow found Ja’Marr Chase in the end zone to give the Bengals a 7-0 lead. Behold:
  • And that touchdown catch Chase made? Not only did Burrow place the ball where no one other than Chase could make a play on it, but Chase somehow contorted his body, made the catch and kept his feet in bounds. It should absolutely be in the conversation for catch of the year when the season comes to an end. Behold again:
  • Orlando Brown Jr. was outmatched on Sunday. He struggled badly protecting Burrow’s blind side, allowing three sacks and committing two penalties. A big reason the offense got off to such a slow start was because Burrow was constantly under pressure, often from behind.
  • Again, the Bengals made a point of putting Burrow under center. The running game looked great when Burrow took the snap directly from Ted Karras with Chase Brown in the backfield. Brown averaged four yards per carry, and as a result, the offense looks much more balanced in 2026 than it did in 2025.
  • While the Bengals’ running game worked when called upon—for the most part—the Texans were absolutely stuffed all day. Running backs David Montgomery and Woody Marks combined for just 18 yards on 14 carries. Making any offense one-dimensional is huge, and the Bengals did exactly that.
  • If the Bengals defense had a weakness on Sunday, it was covering the tight end. Dalton Schultz caught 12 passes for 140 yards.
  • The Bengals’ offensive line was also flagged several times. That’s something they’ll need to clean up.
  • In 2025, the Bengals defense sacked the quarterback three times over the first two weeks of the season. In 2026, they have nine sacks through two games. That puts them on pace for 76 sacks over a 17-game season.
  • Once again, there were waves of pass rushers, and everybody got in on the action. Cedric Johnson had two sacks, while Shemar Stewart and Jonathan Allen each had one. Lawrence didn’t record a sack, but he led the team with an 83.9 pass-rushing grade, per PFF, while adding four hurries. Boye Mafe had eight hurries, and Cashius Howell added five. This isn’t one guy carrying the pass rush. It’s coming from everywhere.
  • Goosebumps…

The Bengals hit the road again in Week 3 as they open AFC North play against the Steelers in Pittsburgh. The Steelers are 1-1 and coming off a loss to the Patriots in Foxborough after defeating the Falcons 20-13 in Week 1.

Pittsburgh, led by Aaron Rodgers, has struggled offensively so far. The Steelers rank 30th in the league in both total offensive yards and points scored. But, in typical Steelers fashion, their defense has been solid. They’ve allowed the 10th-fewest yards and are tied for the eighth-fewest points allowed.

So, we could be looking at a battle of defenses in Week 3.

At the same time, if I have to choose which offense I trust in a defensive slugfest, I’ll almost always choose the one led by Burrow and Chase.

The Bengals opened as 3.5-point favorites in Pittsburgh, and with a win, they would become the 10th team in franchise history to start a season 3-0. The last time it happened was way back in 2015, when we were chanting “MVP” for Andy Dalton before his season was derailed by a broken thumb.

As always, it’s one week at a time, but it’s hard not to be excited about what we’re seeing.

For years, we’ve said things like, “If they could just get off to a hot start, they wouldn’t have to spend the second half of the season trying to dig themselves out of a hole.” Or, “If they could just have a mediocre defense, this offense could take them all the way.”

Well, they’ve gotten off to the hot start.

And they don’t have a mediocre defense.

They have a good one.

Once the offense really gets firing—and we all know it will—watch out.

Now they just need to stay healthy.

Who Dey!

Takin’ care of business

item.title: Ravens news: NFL downplays concerns about Brazil field conditions
item.description: Rounding up the latest news and analysis abut the Baltimore Ravens!
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of all of the latest news and analysis regarding the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover recent concerns about field conditions for the team’s upcoming trip to Brazil, early-season concerns after Sunday’s loss to the Saints, and the officiating pool report on Tyler Shough’s controversial game-winning touchdown.

Ravens’ Week 3 trip to Brazil to proceed as planned

Multiplereports over the weekend raised concerns about the field conditions at Maracaña Stadium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where the Ravens are scheduled to take on the Cowboys next Sunday. Members of CR Flamengo, the home soccer team, have criticized the playing surface, but NFL field director Nick Pappas said on Monday that there are “no concerns right now.”

NFL: ‘No concerns’ over field conditions in Rio for Cowboys-Ravens – Jamison Hensley (ESPN)

‘Look, there’s the realities of managing any playing surface and then there’s also the realities of managing a grass playing surface that’s being used midseason,” Pappas told ESPN on Monday. “So it’s all about monitoring it. It’s all about having a plan in place and then being able to react to anything that maybe comes our way.’

Pappas added, ‘So what we’ve seen in Rio is a significant amount of rainfall, a record kind of rainfall over the last six weeks. And that obviously poses challenges just from a management perspective, but nothing that we’re not capable of managing or prepared to take.’

Ravens-Cowboys in Brazil ‘full speed ahead’ despite field concerns, Stephen Jones says – Jeff Howe, Mike Jones and Dan Pompei (The Athletic)

‘I don’t have concerns only because the league has said full speed ahead. … I think if there was a real concern, there would have already been contingent plans being made,’ [Cowboys co-owner Stephen] Jones said. ‘I know how the league works, about where we play the game if it weren’t there, and there’s none of that. So, I think we’re full speed ahead.‘

‘Whatever work needs to be done on the field to make sure that it’s safe and great for our players, no one understands that more than the league, that we’ve got to have great surfaces and great playing fields that are very safe for our players. As far as I’m concerned, we’re full speed ahead and we’re ready to go to Rio.’

Let’s be realistic here. The NFL has invested heavily in expanding football’s international appeal. It would take something extreme for the league to change their plans for a game featuring one of the most recognizable teams in the world and one of the sport’s biggest stars. The Ravens and the Cowboys will simply have to prepare and adjust.

For Baltimore, that could mean a conservative approach with players dealing with lower-body injuries like Zay Flowers (hamstring) and Ronnie Stanley (toe). Teddye Buchanan (knee) and Nnamdi Madubuike (neck) could also have to wait another week to make their 2026 debuts after months away from the field.

Ravens expected to rebound from Week 2 loss to Saints

NFL Week 2 panic meter: Caleb Williams’ injury, another Chargers no-show shake up early season – Jeff Howe, Mike Jones and Dan Pompei (The Athletic)

Which version of the Baltimore Ravens is closer to reality? The team that blew out the Indianapolis Colts in Week 1 or the group that blew a second-half lead and lost 24-17 to the New Orleans Saints on Sunday?

Pompei: The Ravens’ collapse was rough with self-inflicted wounds, and head coach Jesse Minter’s leadership will be tested early. Their performance was sloppy — not unusual for many teams early in the season. The Ravens have committed 17 penalties in two weeks. That cannot continue if the Ravens are going to be contenders. But this is a talented team that’s capable of high-end football, as they showed in Week 1 against the Colts. It will be a surprise if the Ravens don’t rebound and remain one of the better teams in the AFC. They just need to get in a groove.

Jones: The Ravens are somewhere in the middle, but a smidge closer to the Week 1 product. Many elements of Sunday’s performance resemble the Ravens of last season (penalties and ill-timed turnovers, a couple of head-scratcher offensive play calls, late-game defensive collapse). But the roster and energy within the organization improved. It’s important to remember that Baltimore has a 30-year-old rookie offensive coordinator in Declan Doyle, and that the unit wasn’t at full force with two of Lamar Jackson’s top wide receivers injured.

There were some drops (even one by the reliable Mark Andrews) that, if caught, could have extended drives, and extended drives lead to heavier emphasis on the run. And had Doyle displayed more discipline/patience by giving Derrick Henry the ball on third-and-1 late rather than calling a deep shot downfield, perhaps the Ravens would have kept moving the ball and eventually scored. The Ravens hurt themselves on Sunday, but they’re still one of the better teams in the AFC.

Howe: The Ravens’ inconsistent start is reminiscent of issues with blown leads under the previous regime, ceding control of a winnable game while falling out of sorts in the second half. Jackson and the offense went three-and-out on back-to-back drives while the Saints orchestrated consecutive touchdowns. The Ravens should be in the playoff conversation throughout the season, but I’m curious to see if this team can distinguish itself from past incarnations.

NFL explains officiating call on Tyler Shough’s controversial game-winning touchdown

Pool report with NFL Vice President of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth – Jamison Hensley (ESPN)

Question: Was there clear evidence that Tyler Shough crossed the goal line on the fourth down quarterback sneak (1:32 remaining, New Orleans 4th and 1, Baltimore 1 yard-line)?

Mark Butterworth: “The key here is the ruling on the field is a touchdown. So, we need clear and obvious video evidence that he didn’t score in order to reverse the on-field ruling. We stopped the game, it’s a high-leverage play, we wanted to make sure to either find clear and obvious video evidence that he didn’t score or to confirm the call on the field. We exhausted all available angles and could not prove clear and obvious that he did not break the plane of the goal line.”

Question: During any of the replays, did it show that Tyler Shough lost control of the ball at any point while trying to get the ball across the goal line?

Butterworth: “No. If he did lose control of the ball, we would need to find, after he regained possession, if the ball broke the plane of the goal line. In that mass of players, we weren’t able to find clear and obvious video evidence that the ball did not break the plane of the goal line. Therefore, the ruling on the field stands.”

Ravens get ‘C’ grade for Week 2 showing

NFL Week 2 grades for all 32 teams: Rams earn an ‘A’ for steamrolling Giants on Monday night – John Breech (CBS Sports)

The Ravens’ new offense looked unstoppable in Week 1, but it came crashing back to earth on Sunday. The Ravens had multiple chances to put this game away, but the offense was only able to muster a total of 32 yards on Baltimore’s final three possessions of the game combined. The Ravens also seemed to forget that Derrick Henry existed. Their star running back had just five carries in the second half, including just one in the fourth quarter. With the Ravens leading 14-3 at halftime, it’s surprising that they didn’t lean on Henry more in the second half. One reason the Ravens got rid of John Harbaugh is because of the blown leads in the second half. Well, in his second game on the job, Jesse Minter now has a blown fourth-quarter lead on his resume.

item.title: Detroit Lions stock report: 5 risers, 11 fallers at Bills
item.description: The biggest risers and fallers from the Detroit Lions' experience in the woodchipper against the Buffalo Bills in Week 2
item.content:encoded:
“Back to business” and “R&R—Redemption & Respect”—two of the Detroit Lions’ biggest mantras this offseason—remain all talk.

Two games is an incredibly small sample size, and a short-road game serving as a stadium opener was far from ideal, but nothing about the start of the 2026 season has resembled the stretch from the second half of 2022 through the 2024 season. Dating back to the 45-31 2024 home playoff upset at the hands of the Washington Commanders, the Lions are 10-10 over their last 20 games across the past 20 months. They still haven’t separated themselves from the disappointing 2025 team that preceded them.

Playing arguably the best football player on the planet, in his kingdom, as he opens the new battle arena they built for him, in a rowdy road environment, on short rest, after going to overtime the previous week, turns out not to be an easy task.

Still, the Lions need to start following through on the repeated talk of cleaning things up, making adjustments, and improving.

It’s incredibly early in a long season, though. While we wait for the respect and redemption to begin, let’s check in on the Lions’ Week 2 stock report—with plenty of football runway remaining.

Stock down: Dan Campbell, HC

The traveling Detroit Lions were the less-prepared team from the jump, getting pulverized early and looking nowhere near primetime-ready. Falling behind 21-0 that quickly is unacceptable for a team with the Lions’ lofty ambitions.

So, it turns out it wasn’t only Tyler Shough and Chris Olave who had the Lions’ defense’s number. Josh Allen continued to have his way with Campbell’s defense in what became one of the worst defensive performances of Campbell’s tenure.

The entire team was slow to start and ill-prepared, but the defense is particularly concerning. Through two games, that unit appears to be in its worst shape since Campbell inherited the talent-deficient defense left behind by Matt Patricia.

That’s noteworthy because Campbell spent much of training camp praising his experienced, heady group of veteran defensive backs, who have performed poorly to start the season. More broadly, Campbell has consistently backed his defensive players and coaching staff, including at the NFL Scouting Combine:

“I think Shep did a good job, and I think he learned a lot and I think he grew a ton. I love the staff that’s around him, I really do, man. We’ve just got to tighten the screws on a few things.”

“We’ve already been through the cutup. Like, ‘Man, if we could go back, maybe we would play a little bit more of this or a little less of this.’ I think there’s a lot of clarity in some things. … What can we do better? What do the players — what can they do better? How complex is this, really? Is it out of their wheelhouse? [Are we] asking somebody to do something they cannot do?”

Everything leads to the top. The poor defensive performance and the defensive staff’s lack of preparation ultimately fall on Campbell’s shoulders. It’s on him to make sure his staff is correcting mistakes, tightening up fundamentals, putting players in positions that fit their abilities, and continuing to develop the talent on this defense.

Stock down: Kelvin Sheppard, DC

Through eight quarters, no one in the Detroit Lions organization has been more disappointing than the second-year coordinator, and his unit currently looks like the worst-organized defense in football.

The issues against the Bills ran the full gamut: scrambles, coverage mishaps, wide-open receivers, blitzes that couldn’t get home, third-down woes, red-zone ineptitude, poor angles in run support, read-option struggles, explosive runs, trailing in man coverage, soft zones, free releases, and bad eyes.

Really, nothing the defense did went right. Allen recorded his fourth career game with at least three passing touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns. It was just the 24th such game by a quarterback in NFL history, and Kordell Stewart is the only other quarterback to accomplish the feat more than once. The Bills piled up 34 first downs and 41 points on their first 65 offensive plays alone.

The Lions’ defenders were put in constant conflict, struggling with the positions they were put in and the responsibilities of their assignments. The most disturbing part of Sheppard’s defense Thursday night—and really his entire tenure as a play caller—has been an inability to adapt. When opponents have identified weaknesses and started exploiting them, Sheppard and his staff have failed to find answers for their players. He can rarely find a counterpunch after his defense has been smacked in the mouth. 

The defense now has 10 days to address its woes before taking on Jets QB Geno Smith, who has consistently shredded the Lions in the past. That begins a stretch of three games that appeared manageable all offseason and now represents an opportunity for this defense to figure out what it can actually do successfully before the bye week and the divisional schedule picks up. Perhaps they outsmarted themselves, and it’s time to simplify things. 

All offseason, offenses led by Smith, Bryce Young, and Jacoby Brissett looked like the cupcake portion of the schedule. Now, it’s hard to say with any confidence that this Lions defense will be able to contain any of them.

It’s time for Sheppard and his staff to step up, find answers, and make meaningful corrections. Otherwise, the questions about this defense—and the people responsible for it—are only going to get louder.

Stock down: Jack Campbell, LB

Lions green-dot captain and All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell was highly critical—and emotional—about his performance postgame in the visitors’ locker room in Buffalo, taking responsibility for letting the offense and his teammates down with his struggles.

Campbell has not gotten off on the right foot this season, and those unexpected struggles were put under a microscope against the MVP-caliber, superhuman talent of Josh Allen and Joe Brady’s offense.

Campbell struggled mightily in two areas. He was repeatedly sucked into blocks and unable to fight through or elude them, particularly against the Bills’ tight ends, while also looking lost or a step slow at times in coverage. He also missed a few opportunities to bring down Allen and James Cook.

Campbell’s two-game performance has been incredibly uncharacteristic, arguably his roughest stretch since his rookie season in 2023. Still, there are endless reasons to believe he’ll bounce back and return to playing like one of the best linebackers in football.

Stock up: Jared Goff, QB

If you want reassurance that it’s a long season and the Lions still have promising NFC North title and Super Bowl-contending capabilities, look no further than Jared Goff’s performance over the final three quarters, picking apart the Bills’ defense with precision.

Goff still doesn’t get the credit he deserves, despite dialing in for an impressive 327 passing yards, four touchdowns, a 130.0 passer rating, and 19 passing first downs (tied for seventh most of his career).

He did all of this while routinely facing obvious passing situations behind three backup offensive linemen, leading to a 45.5% pressure rate and four sacks, yet still finding ways to succeed despite the ill-equipped protection.

Goff did it all: maneuvering the pocket and pump-faking to avoid crisis before finding Jahmyr Gibbs or Sione Vaki on checkdowns; firing tight-window throws over the middle to Gibbs and Sam LaPorta; using precision to squeak the ball to Gibbs in the end zone; and dropping timing-and-anticipation dimes to Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and even Isaac TeSlaa along the sideline.

His connection with St. Brown outside the numbers, rather than relying exclusively on their usual bread-and-butter work over the middle, was particularly promising.

Goff playing like that while Buffalo’s defensive front infested his pocket due to the underperforming backups on the offensive line—and doing it with this cast of playmakers around him—is the biggest reason for hope that the Lions can bust out a winning streak before their bye week and put this embarrassment behind them.

Stock down: Devin White & Chuck Clark

There’s a reason White is on his fifth team in four seasons and couldn’t carve out a role on the Texans’ defense two years ago. There’s also a reason Clark is on his third team in three seasons and was only a part-time starter for the Steelers last year.

Both can still be useful coming downhill at times, and Clark is supposedly a good communicator, but at this point, their alleged positive playmaking in those areas doesn’t appear to offset the negatives.

Too often against the Bills, they were liabilities in space—slow-moving statues stuck in the mud. Their age and deteriorating athleticism, combined with some slow processing and hesitation from White, particularly against play action, don’t allow them to cover the necessary depth or ground. At times against Buffalo, their ineffective movement skills made it feel like the Lions’ defense was playing 11-on-9.

Avonte Maddox also had his share of struggles before his season-ending injury. The hope is that none of these veterans will struggle this much against other opponents, with Buffalo’s offense representing one of their toughest matchups, but that isn’t satisfactory.

In the safety room, the best possible solution while waiting out Brian Branch’s return—and possibly Kerby Joseph’s—is to kick Christian Izien back from nickel to handle more safety reps and continue giving Thomas Harper more opportunities. Harper struggled against Buffalo as well, but he has range and a higher ceiling. Relying on the veterans’ floor when the miscommunication issues remain defeats the point.

At linebacker, it’s similarly baffling that White is outsnapping Malcolm Rodriguez by such a significant margin, 33 to 15 on Thursday night. Rodriguez should offer more consistent play, and if he can’t beat White out, then it’s time to get Jimmy Rolder rolling as the third linebacker and WILL. At least there’s room for growth there.

White and Clark on this defense feel much more like Bruce Irvin, David Long Jr., Kwon Alexander, Jamal Adams, Ben Niemann, Dean Marlowe, Jalen Mills, Tre Flowers, or Tyson Alualu band-aid signings than players filling plus roles for a defense expected to ascend as the season wears on.

Stock down: Larry Borom & Ben Bartch

The two offseason investments might’ve been Detroit’s two worst players on either side of the football. Borom never looked this out of sorts in any of his 11 starts with the Miami Dolphins last season, while Bartch never played this poorly across four starts with the San Francisco 49ers over the last two seasons.

Borom had his hands full with Gregory Rousseau, giving up at least eight pressures to him alone, while Bartch was getting bodied by Deone Walker and had poor pass-protection reps against DeWayne Carter, Michael Hoecht, and Bradley Chubb. There was minimal pocket integrity for Goff to rely on given the struggles of both linemen.

As an extra cherry on top: Borom was flagged for a hold and two false starts in the hostile road environment.

Juice Scruggs also struggled much more than he did in his Week 1 debut, as Hank Fraley’s group was collectively out-executed and outmuscled. The hope is that a quick-turnaround road game represents something close to the worst-case scenario for this makeshift offensive line and that Borom and Bartch can improve.

Still, getting Christian Mahogany and Blake Miller back for Week 3 after the long rest would be far better for an offense that needs its offensive line to become the battleship unit capable of destroying everything in its path and carrying this team to success.

Quick Hits

STOCK UP:

  • Tate Ratledge, RG: Ratledge handled his pass-protection reps against the Bills’ interior defenders much better than his fellow offensive linemates while also being a bully in the run game during the first half, before the ground approach shifted mostly to unsuccessful second-down outside zone runs.
  • Amon-Ra St. Brown, WR: It took a second to get going, but St. Brown was one of the biggest reasons the Lions made the game remotely competitive, recording the seventh-most receiving yards of his career (142) as a chunk-play magnet for Goff. It was only his third career game with 120-plus receiving yards and at least two receiving touchdowns.
  • Tyleik Williams, NT: Williams is starting to stack games as a powerful force at the point of attack, occasionally flashing the athleticism to shoot into the backfield while also providing more pass-rush juice than he displayed last season, with another handful of pressures. He forced an awkward Allen incompletion on one pass-rush win and also disrupted the timing of a screen pass.
  • Christian Izien, DB: Looked comfortable operating in the box during a solid Lions debut on only 26 snaps. He made multiple plays stuffing James Cook and looks like a player who needs to see a significant increase in usage.

STOCK DOWN

  • Brock Wright & Tyler Conklin, TEs: The Lions’ backups pale in comparison to the skill sets of Bills backup tight ends Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes, who were blowing open holes in the run game. Aside from Wright’s unfair mismatch on the sack allowed, he continues to be a player who constantly reminds me of Milton Waddams from Office Space, leaving me to ask, “What is it you do here?” Meanwhile, Conklin can’t carve out more than a few reps.
  • D.J. Wonnum, DE: Had a few reps where he got washed out and lost contain in run defense without displaying any pass-rush presence. Right now, he’s been a net-negative player opposite Hutchinson.
  • Tyler Lacy, DL: Maybe there’s a role for him in short-yardage situations, but he’s not a dynamic player, and his lack of movement skills was exposed against the efficient, high-flying Bills offense. The Lions’ defense would be better served by giving up some of his reps to a potential difference-maker in Ahmed Hassanein.
  • Rock Ya-Sin, CB: Ya-Sin is performing like a much more limited, flawed cornerback than he did in the back half of last season or throughout training camp. The off coverage has been a real detriment to his skill set, and consistently losing in the short-to-intermediate areas against Keon Coleman isn’t going to cut it in this division.

STOCK NEUTRAL

  • Drew Petzing, OC: Managed the game well despite being down three offensive linemen on a short week, being taken out of his regular game script early, and still schemed up some really impressive passing concepts for Gibbs and St. Brown. The offense needs to start faster, still hasn’t attacked the intermediate middle of the field much, and the run game remains a work in progress after the Lions posted the worst run-stuff rate by any offense in a game this season. Still, Petzing’s offense is the fourth-highest-scoring unit in football through two weeks. Continue evolving beyond tendencies and growing more comfortable, but there’s plenty here to work with. 
  • Isaac TeSlaa, WR: Better late than never, with his first catch of the season coming on fourth down in the fourth quarter, but he remains a second-year player who hasn’t raised his level of play.
  • Penei Sewell, LT: Sewell will be fine at left tackle. The Kirk Herbstreit broadcast commentary was blown out of proportion after one bad rep against Bradley Chubb.
  • Aidan Hutchinson, DE: The Lions’ best defender and a game-breaking pass rusher showed up from the first drive, unlike many of his teammates. However, he was exposed at times in run defense. Some of that can be attributed to the defensive front being more active with slants and stunts this season, and adjusting there is a broader point for the entire defense given its issues with gap integrity and how effectively the Bills’ extra-tight-end sets took advantage. Hutchinson did kick butt on the goal-line stop of James Cook and clobbered Dion Dawkins on the eventual Barnes cleanup sack. He also nearly got another sack on his menacing, lumbering hawk-down of Allen on a rollout.
  • Derrick Barnes, LB: While he had some initial issues on scramble drills—the entire defense looked unprepared for scramble rules—Barnes was one defender who looked like he belonged against the Bills offense and showed some blitz chops. He ate up D.J. Moore on one end-around. Still too many SAM linebacker reps for my liking.
  • D.J. Reed, CB: Had a very strong game in coverage. The one critique is that while he’s generally a strong run supporter for an undersized cornerback, he took a handful of incorrect or passive angles when filling in run support.

item.title: Horse Tracks: Defense gets back on track
item.description: And just in time before they face a gauntlet of high-powered offenses.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, Broncos Country!

Well, that game was soooo much more fun to watch. A week after getting shredded by the Chiefs, the Broncos defense looked like themselves again, holding the high-powered Jaguars offense to just 13 points.

After a record-setting performance in Week 1 for yards given up due to missed tackles, the defense did not wantn to repeat their abysmal play. And Zach Allen noted that no one on defense expected anything less than a bounce-back game this week.

“We’ve kind of proven that for the past three years now,” Allen said of the team’s ability to rebound from a bad game. “So it’s kind of funny how everyone was freaking out after one game. It’s been like four straight years of slow starts. So luckily we got back on track today.”

The Broncos’ offense couldn’t find the end zone in the first half, despite two trips to the red zone. Following a massive 49-yard catch by Jaylen Waddle at the one, the offense sputtered for three downs and settled for a field goal. Then a Bo Nix interception in the end zone prevented another score and gave the Jaguars a chance to score just before the half.

But Denver’s defense kept the score tight, allowing only field goals the rest of the game after giving up one touchdown at the start of the second quarter.

And that gave the offense time to find some rhythm and put together three second-half scoring drives, including two touchdowns, to finally gain the advantage in the fourth quarter.

Riley Moss’s interception in the third quarter was a big part of keeping the Jaguars from getting too far ahead before the offense could catch up. After the game, Sean Payton noted the takeaway, along with getting off the field on third downs, as keys to holding back Jacksonville.

“That’s a really good offense,” Payton said. “When you looked at last year’s game, I thought they were outstanding. They were going to make their plays, but it was a much different game than a year ago. We had our hands on a few others, but we got off the field on third down. That was good.”

Cornerback Ja’Quan McMillian said the response came from how the group practiced during a short week between games.

“It’s always been the standard,” McMillian said. “We didn’t do that last week. We responded the right way. We had a great week of practice on a short week. Just went out there and kept fighting and got the ‘W.'”

Allen credited better fundamentals for containing Jacksonville’s run game after a rough showing a week earlier.

“Last week wasn’t our standard by any means, but again, guys were like for the most part in the right spots,” he said. “So I think we just tackled a little bit better, swarmed better. Just proud of the group and just got to continue to build off of it. There’s still a lot of things to improve on, and we got a lot of tough games coming up.”

Payton also saw the win as evidence his team has built the mental toughness to handle adversity in close games, pointing to the confidence the team has built from being tested in games like this before.

“I also think there’s a confidence level in a team that because they’ve won before, they’ve been behind before and then how do they respond?” Payton said. “So I think on the positive side, it’s that confidence having been here before, and then from a coaching perspective, ‘Hey, how do we find a way to not be in as many one-score games or behind in one-score games going forward?’ There are some specific areas that we outlined.”

Denver won’t have much time to enjoy the improvement. The Broncos host the Rams on Sunday Night Football this week, who come in after a statement win of their own in Week 2 following an embarrassing Week 1 loss. On Monday Night Football, Matthew Stafford threw for 327 yards and four touchdowns, two to Davante Adams, while the duo rushing attack from Kyren Williams and Blake Corum combined for 164 yards in the Rams 28-6 pummeling of the Giants.

But Allen promises the Broncos aren’t looking past this week’s win and every player knows the tough games coming up.

“We’ve got a really tough opponent this upcoming week,” he said. “So can’t afford any slow starts or lapses, so just got to get going.”

item.title: Terps in the NFL Week 2: Diggs scores twice for Commanders in gutting loss to Cowboys
item.description: See how Maryland football alumni fared in a low-scoring second week of NFL play.
item.content:encoded:
Week 2 of the NFL season concluded with 12 Maryland football alumni seeing the field. 

Washington Commanders wide receiver Stefon Diggs recorded his best game with the team against the Dallas Cowboys Sunday. Diggs had two touchdowns, five catches and 47 yards on six targets. 

Diggs’ first score came on a redzone four-yard flat route from quarterback Jayden Daniels. His second score was a tight double coverage catch while falling on the endzone sideline in the fourth quarter. 

His two scores brought him to 77 career touchdowns. He is tied with Joey Galloway for 38th all-time on the receiving touchdowns list. The Gaithersburg, Maryland, native is now four scores away from the top 35, where he would tie Oakland Raiders great Art Powell and Carolina Panthers legend Steve Smith Sr. at 81.  

While he gets settled in Washington, Diggs and the team will likely have to navigate the foreseeable future without Daniels. The franchise quarterback suffered a dislocated left elbow just before halftime. There are no fractures, but he is expected to miss time. Daniels missed roughly a month in 2025 with the same elbow issue. 

The Commanders, now 0-2, will rely on a veteran group that includes Diggs to help the team not fall too far behind. Through two weeks, the 32-year-old leads the offense in catches, yards and touchdowns. 

Washington will host the Seattle Seahawks Sunday at 1 p.m. in its home opener.  

2026 alumni 

  • Jacksonville Jaguars safety Jalen Huskey was an inactive healthy scratch against the Denver Broncos in Week 2. 
  • New Orleans Saints offensive lineman Alan Herron remained on the practice squad for Week 2. 

Players

  • Buffalo Bills wide receiver DJ Moore sustained an AC joint sprain Thursday against the Detroit Lions. He attempted to catch an endzone pass and landed hard on his left shoulder. Moore left in the second quarter and is considered day-to-day. There is a chance he plays against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3.
  • Commanders safety Nick Cross made three tackles against the Cowboys. However, he was hospitalized postgame and evaluated for an internal injury. Cross stayed overnight but was discharged Monday and traveled back to Ashburn, Virginia. His Week 3 status is uncertain. 
  • Miami Dolphins safety Dante Trader Jr. made two tackles against the San Francisco 49ers. 
  • Chargers cornerback Tarheeb Still made two tackles against the Las Vegas Raiders. 
  • Dolphins defensive tackle Jordan Phillips made one tackle against the 49ers. 
  • Atlanta Falcons linebacker Josh Woods made one tackle against the Carolina Panthers. 
  • Arizona Cardinals kicker Chad Ryland converted one extra point against the Seahawks. 
  • Raiders offensive lineman DJ Glaze received a 56.6 overall grade in blocking from Pro Football Focus against the Chargers. He played all offensive snaps.  
  • Pittsburgh Steelers offensive lineman Spencer Anderson played 67 snaps and received a 59 blocking grade via PFF against the New England Patriots. 
  • Panthers offensive lineman Corey Bullock played 11 snaps against the Falcons. 
  • Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Tai Felton saw time on special teams against the Chicago Bears. 
  • New York Giants cornerback Deonte Banks was inactive with a calf injury on Monday Night Football against the Los Angeles Rams. Banks did not practice Friday and Saturday. He worked out pregame but was ruled out prior to kickoff. 
  • Commanders tight end Chig Okonkwo was inactive against the Cowboys. He suffered a hamstring injury in Week 1.
  • Bills running back Ty Johnson was inactive with a hamstring injury against the Lions. Johnson has yet to play this season. 

Practice squad & injured reserve 

  • Commanders defensive tackle Byron Cowart remained on the practice squad for Week 2. 
  • Dolphins offensive lineman Gottlieb Ayedze remained on the practice squad for Week 2. 
  • Chargers offensive lineman Josh Kaltenberger remained on the practice squad for Week 2. 
  • 49ers defensive end Sam Okuayinonu remained on injured reserve due to early September foot surgery. The team is hoping for a late season return. 
  • Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Jakorian Bennett remained on injured reserve with a knee injury. He is eligible to return in Week 5 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. 
  • Bears linebacker Ruben Hyppolite II remained on injured reserve following shoulder surgery. Hyppolite was waived with an injury designation on Aug. 30, he went unclaimed and reverted back to the team’s IR. He cannot play unless he reaches an injury settlement with the Bears. 

Other notes 

  • Vikings wide receiver Jeshaun Jones remained suspended through Week 3 for violating the NFL’s substance policy. He is eligible for reinstation on Sept. 28. 
  • Longtime Terps running back Roman Hemby remained on the Raiders practice squad for Week 2. 

Week 3 of the NFL season begins Thursday with the Atlanta Falcons at Green Bay Packers on Prime.
